items.title: One day after MacKinnon called Bill C-39 a ‘slam dunk,’ PM Carney says he will whip votes
items.description: The prime minister's position is a far cry from comments the House leader made in an interview with CTV Question Period, where he called the bill a 'slam dunk.'
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney (left) and Government House leader Steven MacKinnon in the House of Commons, Thursday, May 29, 2025 in Ottawa. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The prime minister's position is a far cry from comments the House leader made in an interview with CTV Question Period, where he called the bill a 'slam dunk.'
items.body:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Liberals will whip the vote for his government’s omnibus Bill C-39, just one day after Government House leader Steven MacKinnon told CTV News he was confident the legislation would pass without doing so.

“You’re a member of the party, and so we will vote as a government in that,” Carney said while speaking to reporters in Yellowknife on Friday.

A whipped vote refers to a legislative vote in which political party members are expected or required to vote according to their party leadership’s instructions.

Carney also described the bill as “the most important economic legislation that we have.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The prime minister’s position is a far cry from comments MacKinnon made Thursday in an interview with CTV Question Period, in which the government House leader described the bill as a “slam dunk with our own MPs.”

The full interview with MacKinnon will air Sunday.

In an opinion piece published in the Toronto Star, however, B.C.-based Liberal MP Will Greaves wrote that he is “worried” Canada is losing its climate credibility and wouldn’t say earlier this week whether he would support Bill C-39.

Asked explicitly by host Vassy Kapelos if the party will whip the vote, MacKinnon vigorously insisted that wouldn’t be necessary.

“I don’t think we have to whip the vote,” MacKinnon told Kapelos. “This is a bill that we all, the principles on which we all ran. We all got elected, and we’re very, very proud to be able to hold this bill up as an example of the great things we can get done for our country.”

Bill C-39 — also known as the Building Canada Strong Act — is designed to speed up federal approvals for major projects and revise federal labour laws. A House of Commons committee struck to examine C-39 wrapped earlier this week with minor changes made after a marathon study.

But the landmark legislation has garnered criticism for weakening environmental safeguards, infringing on Indigenous rights, restricting workers’ right to strike and rushing parliamentary scrutiny.

All opposition parties have signalled they will not support the bill. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is the latest opposition leader to state his position, saying on Thursday that his party will vote against the legislation after the Liberals refused to accept major changes.

Without opposition support, Liberals will need all the party’s MPs to vote in favour of the legislation for it to pass, as they hold a razor thin majority with 173 seats.

This press release is provided by GlobeNewswire and is published as received.

TORONTO, Nov. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Purpose Investments Inc. (“Purpose”) is pleased to share that the Longevity Pension Fund (“Longevity” or “the Fund”) is again raising its distribution levels for all of its F-series and A-series cohorts in 2027. Longevity is the world’s first income-for-life mutual fund designed to provide income security for retired Canadians.

“In its fifth year of operation, the Longevity Pension Fund continues to deliver on its mandate,” says Fraser Stark, President of Longevity Retirement Platform at Purpose Investments. “Following another year of above-expectation portfolio returns for the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, funding levels remain above our target levels. Our Income Policy, therefore, calls for another increase in distribution levels in 2027. We’re delighted to see the impact this has on our investors and their ability to spend with confidence in retirement.”

The third consecutive increase in distribution levels highlights the strength of the Fund’s unique structure. The specific changes in distribution level for each cohort for 2027 are as follows: 

These levels are determined by Longevity’s Income Policy, published in 2022, which describes how distribution levels are managed and by how much they may be adjusted under a range of possible future scenarios. “We take a funding-level approach to managing the distribution levels with the goal of matching assets and liabilities,” says Stark. “Our actively managed, pension-style portfolio achieved an impressive 12-month net return of 7.81% (series AF – representative series of the underlying portfolio)1 as of September 30, 2026, and that contributes strongly to this increase for 2027.”

An important element of the Income Policy is that distribution level increases are capped at 3% year over year during the early years of each cohort’s lifecycle. This is designed to help stabilize distribution levels and effectively splits any excess funding ratio between raising next year’s income and building a buffer for stability in later years.

Over the coming weeks, Purpose will publish the Fund’s 2026 Annual Report, aiming to demonstrate that Purpose follows the approach as described in the Income Policy, add clarity on how the Fund’s distribution levels are expected to evolve over the lifecycle of a cohort based on its current circumstances, and validate that Longevity is on track to achieve its objective of providing lifetime income.

About Longevity Pension Fund

The Longevity Pension Fund is the world’s first income-for-life mutual fund, combining longevity risk pooling with a diversified investment portfolio to provide lifetime income for Canadian retirees through variable monthly distributions that are designed to grow over time. For more information about Longevity and Purpose’s mission to help Canadians redefine retirement with income for life, visit RetireWithLongevity.com.

CALGARY, Alberta, Nov. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Athabasca Oil Corporation (TSX: ATH) (“Athabasca” or the “Corporation”) is pleased to announce that its proposed arrangement with Cenovus Energy Inc. For additional details of the voting results on the Transaction Resolution, see Athabasca’s Report of Voting Results filed pursuant to Section 11.3 of National Instrument 51-102 – Continuous Disclosure Obligations available on Athabasca’s profile on SEDAR+ at www.sedarplus.ca.

items.body:
This press release is provided by GlobeNewswire and is published as received.

TORONTO, Nov. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan (HOOPP) today announced that Michael Wissell, Chief Investment Officer, will retire on January 15, 2027. Shrirang Apte, currently Senior Managing Director, Head of Capital Markets, will succeed him as Chief Investment Officer.

Mr. Wissell joined HOOPP in 2018 and was named Chief Investment Officer in 2021. Throughout that time, he strengthened HOOPP’s investment capabilities, introduced new strategies and helped advance the evolution of the investment organization and its Total Portfolio Approach. The Plan’s assets grew from $77 billion to over $132 billion over the course of his tenure.

“Michael has been a thoughtful and trusted leader whose judgment, experience and commitment to our members have had a lasting impact on HOOPP,” said Annesley Wallace, HOOPP’s Chief Executive Officer. “He has played an important role in the evolution of our investment organization and leaves behind a strong team and foundation for the future. On behalf of everyone at HOOPP, I want to thank Michael for his leadership and the many contributions he has made to the Plan.”

“HOOPP’s purpose has always been personal to me,” said Mr. Wissell. “I am proud of what we have accomplished together and the strength of the team. It has been a privilege to serve HOOPP and its members.”

Mr. Apte has been with HOOPP since 2006, when he joined to establish Global Credit as an asset class. Since 2023, as Head of Capital Markets, he has led an integrated platform covering the Plan’s public assets and private credit. His appointment reflects HOOPP’s long-term approach to succession planning and developing leadership depth within the Investment Management team. He holds the CFA designation, earned a Bachelor of Engineering from MS University (India) and an MBA from Wilfrid Laurier University.

“Strong succession planning is critical to the long-term strength of an investment organization,” said Ms. Wallace. “Over two decades at HOOPP, Shrirang has taken on progressively broader investment and leadership responsibilities. He brings broad investment judgment, a deep understanding of our portfolio and investment philosophy, and a demonstrated ability to bring teams and investment capabilities together. I have every confidence in his ability to lead our Investment Management team and continue advancing our Total Portfolio Approach.”

“It is a privilege to take on this responsibility and to build on the strong foundation Michael and the Investment Management team have established,” said Mr. Apte. “HOOPP has exceptional investment capabilities and people across the organization. I look forward to working with the team to continue exercising disciplined investment judgment and delivering the long-term outcomes our members depend on.”

Mr. Wissell will work closely with Mr. Apte through the transition. Mr. Apte will continue to lead Capital Markets and will share plans for the team’s leadership in due course.

About the Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan

HOOPP serves Ontario’s hospital and community-based healthcare sector, with more than 870 participating employers. Its membership includes nurses, medical technicians, food services staff, housekeeping staff, physicians and many others who provide valued healthcare services. In total, HOOPP has more than 504,000 active, deferred and retired members.

HOOPP is fully funded and manages a highly diversified portfolio of $132 billion in assets that span multiple geographies and asset classes. HOOPP is also a major contributor to the Canadian economy, paying more than $4.1 billion in pension benefits annually.

HOOPP operates as a private independent trust, and its Board of Trustees governs the Plan and Fund, focusing on HOOPP’s mission to deliver on its pension promise. The Board is made up of appointees from the Ontario Hospital Association (OHA) and four unions: the Ontario Nurses’ Association (ONA), the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE), the Ontario Public Service Employees’ Union (OPSEU) and the Service Employees International Union (SEIU). This governance model provides representation from both employers and members in support of the long-term interests of the Plan.

items.title: Mackenzie Valley Highway becomes first major project of national interest in Canada’s North
items.description: The government says the 800-km proposed highway would improve access for more than 10,000 people, including providing year-round road access to 2,000 people in the three N.W.T. communities
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney meets with Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson at the legislature in Yellowknife, N.W.T., Thursday, March 12, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The government says the 800-km proposed highway would improve access for more than 10,000 people, including providing year-round road access to 2,000 people in the three N.W.T. communities
items.body:
OTTAWA - Prime Minister Mark Carney has officially deemed the Mackenzie Valley Project as a project of national interest, the first in Canada’s north.

“Today, we are preparing to go further and to grow faster,” said Carney, speaking in Yellowknife.

The government says the 800-kilometre proposed highway would improve access for more than 10,000 people, including providing year-round road access to 2,000 people in the three Northwest Territories (N.W.T.) communities of Tulita, Norman Wells and Fort Good Hope for the first time.

The government estimates a trip between Yellowknife and Inuvik will take 23 hours instead of 38, by cutting out 1,300 kilometres of travel time. It will take 900 fewer kilometres to get from Inuvik to Edmonton.

Carney referenced being born in Fort Smith, N.W.T., and said for the first year of his life the only route out was a winter road. He noted the “opportunity” that followed when an all-weather road was built.

“These connections bring strength,” Carney said.

The highway would run the length of the Mackenzie Valley in the N.W.T., linking Highway 1 at Wrigley and connect with the Dempster Highway, south of Inuvik. The government says the project also requires new bridges to be built, including across the Great Bear, Liard and Mackenzie rivers.

“It will connect communities and lower the cost of living in one of Canada’s most expensive regions, with prices most Canadians couldn’t even dream of,” N.W.T. Premier R. J. Simpson said at the announcement.

“Of course, the region is also home to world-class mineral and petroleum resources, and the highway is key to unlocking those.”

The government estimates the construction price for the northern and southern sections to be $4.2 billion. That does not include the costs of the new bridges nor ongoing maintenance, which could be substantial.

The recent federal budget earmarked $3.1 billion for the highway over the next five years. The budget promises to “fully fund the construction and certain maintenance costs” of the highway.

Officials at a technical briefing for reporters ahead of the announcement, could not say how much in maintenance costs the government is prepared to cover, nor for how long.

Ottawa has also promised to launch a new Crown corporation to manage major projects including the highway. The budget earmarked $187 million over the next five years for the entity, and $24 million in future years. It’s not clear when exactly that entity will be functioning.

New highway’s prospective benefits

The government believes the highway would substantially impact the N.W.T.’s GDP, reduce freight costs, stabilize the cost of living and open up trade in the N.W.T., as well as with other provinces and territories. The highway is also expected to boost tourism by providing a new scenic route through the N.W.T. and Yukon.

In terms of security and defence, the government says the highway will support the Canadian Armed Forces to move more easily and help build defence infrastructure in the North. An official at the briefing said that “global shifts in geopolitics and security are contributing to new vulnerabilities for the Arctic and North region,” and that Canada must “act ambitiously” to “demonstrate its sovereignty in the region.”

The highway project has been a topic of discussions and debates for decades. However, the Carney government takes credit for moving it along “at a pace not seen in generations,” according to a news release announcing a $405-million cash injection in September. That funding includes some money towards the three bridges.

Related construction is already underway, including work to resurface Highway 1 toward Wrigley. The Oscar Bridge relocation and Christina Creek realignment will start once the winter road is built in early 2027.

What comes next?

The government says next steps include finishing an environmental assessment that first began in 2013 and continued Indigenous consultations, although government sources said they were satisfied they had “fulfilled the duty to consult” when making the decision to list the project one of national interest.

Officials said they expect the environmental review to wrap by the end of 2027, noting some “challenges” in terms of being able to meet some communities in person.

More drugs, alcohol access ‘key concern’

In community consultations done so far, government officials said “a really key concern” is around the ease of drugs and alcohol coming into communities, as well as a lack of policing. The official said the federal government is committed to “supporting where we can,” and that the government of the N.W.T. will be working with communities and organizations along the route to address this.

“This is something that we are giving a great deal of thought to,” said Carney at the announcement.

Wednesday, the federal government signed a framework deal for co-leadership, called a Leadership and Governance Understanding (LGU), with Gwich’in Tribal Council, Sahtu Secretariat Incorporated, Pehdzéh Ki First Nation and the Government of the Northwest Territories (GNWT).

The LGU aims to have as much Indigenous participation and job opportunities for northern businesses and workers as possible.

“It includes shared leadership and shared governance, and it helps prepare communities for the opportunities ahead,” Carney said of the LGU.

At the peak of construction, the major projects office estimates the project will need 3,000 workers.

“As a government, we’re working hard to ensure that everyone in the Northwest Territories who is willing and able to work is given that opportunity,” said Simpson, acknowledging the project will need to bring in some outside help as well.

Listing a project in the national interest is supposed to speed up the entire process and streamline federal approvals.

The highway is the third project to officially be deemed in the national interest, along with the Pacific Link pipeline between Alberta and B.C., and the Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion in Delta, B.C.

items.title: Trump encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to exit OPEC: Reuters exclusive
items.description: The U.S. pressured Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC, sources say, in a move that could reshape the global oil market and weaken the group.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A pedestrian walks past a mural featuring oil wells in Caracas, Venezuela, Saturday, Aug 29, 2026, a day after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal giving the United States a stake in Venezuela’s oil reserves. (AP Photo/Pedro Mattey)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Pedro Mattey</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The U.S. pressured Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC, sources say, in a move that could reshape the global oil market and weaken the group.
items.body:
LONDON/BAGHDAD/HOUSTON — The Trump administration encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries earlier this year and prevented Venezuela from paying its annual membership dues to the group, according to 10 people familiar with the matter.

The previously unreported moves targeted two of OPEC’s five founding members, marking an unusually direct challenge to an organization U.S. President Donald Trump has long accused of keeping oil prices artificially high.

U.S. officials were pushing for greater oil production and investment in both countries at the time, and some worried OPEC production limits could eventually constrain those ambitions, according to people familiar with the discussions.

  • Latest updates on international news here

The U.S. pressure on Venezuela went far enough that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened this summer, persuading the Trump administration not to press the issue further, two people familiar with the matter said.

In Iraq, Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi raised the possibility of leaving OPEC at a government meeting this summer after discussions with U.S. officials who encouraged the idea, two people familiar with the matter said.

Iraq’s oil ministry pushed back, persuading al-Zaidi to keep Iraq in the group and consider seeking a higher production quota instead, the people said.

The United States has powerful leverage over both countries. The U.S. controls Venezuela’s access to state funds following the January ouster of Nicolas Maduro, while Iraq’s oil revenues continue to pass through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, a relic of the 2003 Iraq War.

The U.S. State Department did not answer questions about whether it had prevented Venezuela from paying its OPEC membership fee. But it confirmed Washington has the power to decide on Venezuela’s use of state funds, now held in a U.S.-controlled account set up after Maduro’s removal.

“The Department receives disbursement requests from the interim Venezuelan government and reviews the requests, including against a list of approved and prohibited uses of the foreign Government Deposit Funds,” a State Department official told Reuters.

The official said that it was possible that lower-level U.S. officials had raised the question of leaving OPEC with Venezuela’s government earlier this year, but that “it has not been among the issues raised by high-level officials.”

The State Department’s conversations with Iraq, meanwhile, “have focused on improving energy infrastructure to increase production and transportation of energy, not OPEC,” the official said.

Representatives for OPEC and for the governments of Venezuela, Iraq and Saudi Arabia did not respond to requests for comment.

The U.S. manoeuvres add strain to an organization that has already lost four members since 2019, and whose share of the global oil market recently hit a low on the back of disruptions caused by the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran, another OPEC founding member.

“The risk of OPEC fracture is rising,” said Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro.

The United Arab Emirates announced its exit from OPEC earlier this year after becoming frustrated with the group’s production caps, while Angola, Ecuador and Qatar quit the group in 2024, 2020 and 2019, respectively. There are no indications the U.S. was involved in those decisions.

Customer to competitor

OPEC was founded in Baghdad in September 1960 by oil producer countries seeking to assert more control over a global market that had become dominated by a small handful of Western oil companies.

Founded by Iraq, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Venezuela, OPEC is now made up of 11 members. It has also developed an alliance with several other producer countries including Russia called OPEC+, which regularly meets to decide on coordinated production levels.

Trump has repeatedly attacked OPEC throughout his decades-long business and political career, calling it a cartel and a monopoly profiting from the rest of the world. Over the past decade, though, the U.S. has become the world’s largest oil producer, turning it from an OPEC customer into its main rival for oil market share.

  • Latest updates on commodities here

After the U.S. seized Maduro in January, the U.S. State Department opened discussions with Venezuelan officials in Washington on whether the country should leave OPEC, five people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

They did not identify the individuals who took part in those discussions.

Trump wanted U.S. oil majors to revive Venezuela’s oil output - something he said would shore up energy security in the Western Hemisphere - and worried that OPEC policy decisions could hinder that plan, the sources said.

Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened, however, persuading the Trump administration not to push further, two of the sources said. Saudi Arabia is OPEC’s top producer and its de facto leader.

In August, Trump said it was up to Venezuela whether to leave OPEC.

U.S. officials this summer also held talks with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi, encouraging Iraq’s departure from OPEC as U.S. oil majors Exxon Mobil and Chevron planned major new investments there, two people familiar with the matter said.

Al-Zaidi later raised the issue at a government meeting. His oil ministry persuaded him to stay and instead potentially seek a higher OPEC quota, they said.

The issue could come up again since some elements of Iraq’s ruling coalition are favourable to leaving OPEC and OPEC+, which they view as dominated by Saudi Arabia and Russia, the people said.

There is no indication Washington has sought to block Baghdad’s OPEC dues.

After the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003, the United States began routing Iraq’s oil revenues through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. That structure remains in place more than two decades later.

This year, the U.S. threatened to starve Iraq of its oil money if it didn’t cut Iran’s influence in its government.

‘More important matters’

OPEC membership fee payments are typically due in the first quarter of each year, and pay for staff salaries, research, and travel at the OPEC Secretariat in Vienna.

Unlike the United Nations, where dues are scaled to the size of a country’s economy, OPEC splits the fees equally among members at around 2.8 million euros (US$3.08 million) each.

The price tag is tiny compared to OPEC oil revenues, but paying it carries symbolic importance as a marker of continued membership in an organization Caracas helped create.

Washington argued money from Venezuela could be spent on more important matters, one of the people familiar with the country’s relationship with OPEC said.

OPEC has the discretion to disregard unpaid membership fees, and is not planning to expel Venezuela over the issue, two OPEC sources told Reuters.

Washington’s control of Venezuela’s oil revenues and finances has led some in the South American country to refer to their country as a U.S. protectorate, instead of a sovereign nation.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office opened a formal investigation in July into the administration’s management and disbursement of Venezuelan oil revenues, following congressional requests for transparency.

The Trump administration has said Venezuela’s oil revenues are being used to meet the needs of the Venezuelan people, including to pay government salaries and fund essential services.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

Reuters could not establish when exactly the U.S. rejected the OPEC dues payment request.

Venezuela is currently exempt from OPEC+ oil output quotas as its production has collapsed from historical highs due to years of sanctions and mismanagement.

The country pumped about 1.2 million barrels per day in September, according to OPEC figures. Its state oil company PDVSA has said it plans to reach 1.5 million barrels per day by the end of next year.

OPEC last regulated Caracas’ output with quotas in 2017 to 2018 when the country’s target was around 2 million barrels per day. The country’s return to the quota system is unlikely until it hits that level again, a source familiar with Venezuela’s OPEC position said.

items.body:
ASUNCION, Paraguay — Paraguay’s former economy minister Carlos Fernandez Valdovinos turned himself in on Friday, becoming the latest ex-official placed under arrest following the collapse of one of the country’s largest banks.

The Ueno Bank crisis, which saw millions locked out of their life savings earlier this month, has already prompted the ouster of president Santiago Pena, who has been arrested along with several other former top officials.

An arrest warrant for Valdovinos seen by AFP accused the 61-year-old of “alleged criminal acts of administration for personal gain, aggravated passive bribery, criminal association, and money laundering.”

The public prosecutor’s office alleged that while minister in July 2025, he approved the transfer of tens of millions of dollars in pension fund money to Ueno Bank.

He left office in August, after which he signed a multi-million dollar consulting contract with the business group that controlled Ueno Bank.

Prosecutors believe the lucrative contract may have been linked to the pension fund transaction.

The post Canadian Mortgage Arrears Make Biggest Jump In a Decade, Led by $850k+ Loans appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: CMHC and Equifax data shows Canada’s $850k+ mortgage arrears surged to 0.67% in Q2 2026—nearly 3x the rate of small loans—as risk inversion spreads.
items.body:
Canada’s real estate industry is finding out that more leverage wasn’t the solution to high home prices. CMHC and Equifax data shows arrears on the largest mortgages surged in Q2 2026, hitting nearly triple the rate of the smallest loans. What started as a warning sign has turned into full-blown risk inversion—and now it’s spreading.

Risk Inversion: Expected and Unexpected Mortgage Losses

In a typical risk scenario, delinquencies tend to concentrate in smaller loans. This makes sense, since credit access is based on perceived risk, in order to control losses. The riskiest borrowers have the smallest loans; less risk means more credit access. Lenders plan for losses among smaller loans and have prepared for that scenario. Everything is working as expected when this happens, so no need to worry. However, that’s not what’s happening today.

As previously mentioned, risk inversion began to occur in 2023. Smaller mortgage originations began to outperform the largest, with each larger one delivering bigger losses. That trend is continuing into the latest mortgage data.

Canada’s Largest Mortgages Just Saw Their Fastest Delinquency Jump on Record

Canadian mortgage arrears by size of loan at origination.

Source: CMHC; Equifax; Better Dwelling.

The arrears rate for mortgages of $850,000 or more climbed a mind-boggling 8 basis points (bps) in just one quarter to 0.67% in Q2 2026. The rate is 48.9% higher than last year, and nearly 8.4x its 2022 low. This isn’t just a new recent high—it’s the fastest quarterly acceleration in at least 10 years.

To put the climb into perspective, back in April, we flagged this issue when the same tier hit 0.55% in Q4 2025. It was more than double the default rate of the smallest loans under $200,000 (0.23%). Just two quarters later, the gap has widened to 2.8x the arrears rate of loans under $200,000 (0.24%). Even more telling: every loan bracket above $200,000 posted its largest quarterly jump on record in Q2 2026.

Mortgage Stress Is No Longer Just a “Rich Borrower” Problem

When the trend first appeared, it was easy for policymakers and the industry to dismiss the issue. Just overleveraged investors and high-income households who got swept into the exuberance. However, the latest data makes it clear this isn’t the case as the stress cascades down the loan ladder.

Mortgage arrears for the $600,000 to $850,000 bracket jumped 5 bps in Q2 to 0.40%, up a third from last year and nearly 6x its 2022 low. That puts it at 1.7x the default rate of the smallest mortgages. Meanwhile, the $400,000 to $600,000 tier—standard urban mortgage territory—climbed to 0.23%, past its 2017 high (0.22%). The segment is just shy of the arrears rate for the smallest loans that are supposed to be “riskier.” What started as risk inversion at the top of the market is bleeding across most segments.

Despite throwing billions at the problem and turning a blind eye to inflated appraisals to get deals across the line, the strategy is running out of road. Larger loans aren’t just defaulting faster—they’re dragging down the mid-level market too. The safest mortgages defaulting at almost 3x the rate of the riskiest doesn’t just confirm that affordability policies failed. It’s a sign that those policies have created a systemic risk.

The post Canadian Mortgage Delinquencies Rise, Led By Bigger Loans: TransUnion appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian mortgage delinquencies are climbing, led by larger loans. With rate relief off the table, TransUnion warns 2027 renewals risk amplifying stress.
items.body:
The Canadian real estate industry got more bad news this week, this time on the mortgage front. TransUnion data shows that mortgage credit grew in Q3 2026, but with fewer borrowers. Larger loans are driving the trend, with the biggest balances disproportionately fueling delinquencies. Now with rate relief off the table in 2027, lenders are bracing for things to get worse before they improve.

Fewer Mortgage Borrowers, Bigger Loans

Canadian mortgage debt is hitting new highs, despite fewer households carrying a mortgage. TransUnion data shows mortgage balances hit $1.96 trillion in Q3 2026, up 3.4% from last year. The balance represents 74% of the record $2.66 trillion in household debt reported to the bureau. However, active mortgage accounts slipped 0.5% to 6.6 million, while total mortgage holders fell 0.4% to 8.6 million.

That means the balance is growing due to larger mortgages, not more homeowners. The average mortgage balance hit $296,979, 3.9% higher than last year. New originations in Q2 (latest) drove the trend, averaging $374,562, up 4.2% from last year. Mortgage debt is concentrating around existing owners, not a broad expansion of ownership as seen in healthy markets.

Bigger Balances Lead Mortgage Delinquencies, Borrowers Tap Equity

More mortgage borrowers are cracking, according to the bureau’s data. The 60+ day delinquency rate climbed 4 basis points (bps) from last year to 0.31% of accounts and 0.33% of mortgage holders. The share of delinquent balances also climbed 6 bps over the period to 0.33%, outpacing both. The gap suggests that larger mortgages are disproportionately driving the delinquency trend.

Rising delinquencies won’t be calming soon, as there’s significant pressure building. Across all credit products, early 30+ day delinquencies fell to 4.3%, 6 bps lower than last year. However, the 60+ and 90+ day arrears both rose 3 bps to 2.6% and 1.8%, respectively. Fewer newly missed payments is good news, but borrowers who do fall behind are increasingly getting stuck.

Meanwhile, homeowners are leveraging their homes for more variable-rate debt—on top of their mortgages. Total line of credit balances rose 5.8% from last year to $300.8 billion, while new limits surged to an average of $92,489 in Q2 (latest), up 14.7% from last year. TransUnion specifically notes that this is driven heavily by what it calls “likely secured lending” above $80,000.

Collision Course With 2027 Renewals

TransUnion warns the biggest threat is upcoming mortgage renewals, not today’s delinquencies. Borrowers are set to renew with much bigger balances than in previous years, and many at higher rates. Newer originations with larger balances face far greater sensitivity to payment increases. The bureau notes that renewals won’t initiate mortgage deterioration—they risk amplifying existing stress.

That collision is happening just as rate relief has vanished. The Bank of Canada (BoC) hiked its policy rate 25 bps to 2.50% in October—its first increase since 2023. Both RBC and BMO are forecasting another rate hike in December, following a hawkish speech from the BoC governor this week. RBC and Scotiabank now project rates will climb as high as 3.25% in 2027. Lenders will be watching closely to see if higher renewal rates accelerate delinquencies.

items.title: Canadian Mortgage Awards: All the winner reaction from a landmark night
items.description: Winners from the CMAs' 20th anniversary share their thoughts on a memorable occasion in Toronto
items.content: <p>Winners from the CMAs' 20th anniversary share their thoughts on a memorable occasion in Toronto</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639313046166075122.jpeg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Winners from the CMAs' 20th anniversary share their thoughts on a memorable occasion in Toronto
items.body:
The Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) marked their 20th anniversary on Wednesday evening with a landmark gala at Rebel Toronto, as hundreds of mortgage professionals gathered to celebrate the industry's top performers across 25 award categories.

From broker of the year honours to lifetime achievement recognition, the milestone event brought together some of Canada's most prominent lending professionals for a night that highlighted both the industry's resilience and its depth of talent.

Brokers in the spotlight

Rakhee Dhingra of Mortgage Savvy claimed two of the night's most coveted prizes, winning Broker of the Year for Regional, Eastern Canada (Quebec and Ontario) and, later in the evening, the CIMBC Award for Canadian Broker of the Year – the top individual broker honour of the night.

"I've absolutely enjoyed every moment of being in this industry, the learning, the challenges, the ups and the downs," she said after collecting the Eastern Canada award. "The fact that I get to wake up every day and do something I'm passionate about but still impact people's lives in such a meaningful way is such a gift."

Dhingra said her approach to the job is centred around connecting clients with their broader life goals. "It's about guiding clients through understanding how to use their mortgage to build the life they want to live," she said. "Being consistent, focusing on credibility, integrity, and trust, building a system and controls so you can continue to nurture those relationships — that's key."

After claiming the national honour, Dhingra offered profound words for industry members starting their career journey: "We have such a blessed opportunity to impact and create change, but also to create incredible lives for our families."

David Clarke of TMG The Mortgage Group won the Canadian Mortgages Inc. Award for Broker of the Year – Private Lending, an honour he had been nominated for before but had not yet collected. "I'm pretty excited about it," he said.

Clarke said a disciplined, data-driven approach had been essential throughout his year. "I figured out the amount of activities you've got to do to hit a certain result, and I just really follow the math of it."

His edge, he said, comes from building plans around realistic client behaviour: "I think sometimes plans are based off of somebody doing a complete 180, and I just don't think that works for most people. If somebody already spends their credit cards, there's a good chance they're going to again. You've got to build a plan that has the human in it."

Parminder Bhatti of AKAL Mortgages Inc. claimed the EQ Bank Award for Broker of the Year – Reverse Mortgages, winning a category introduced to the CMAs for the first time this year.

"I've been working with seniors for the last six years," said Bhatti, who dedicated the win to mentors he credited with inspiring his work in the reverse mortgage space. "It's a great time to have this category introduced."

Stephen Thomas of Mortgage Alliance HALO Mortgage Advisory took home the Grechi Carter Professional Corporation Award for Broker of the Year – Commercial, crediting an advice-first philosophy for his success.

"It's really just sticking to my purpose, which is providing advice to my borrowers," he said. "Whether I'm able to provide a solution or not, I can still provide advice to save people time and energy and effort and stress."

For Thomas, consistency is the strategy: "A lot of brokers will try to just fit a square peg into a round hole. If you can just keep advice and be efficient, you can save people a lot of stress and give them options."

Lending excellence recognised

Ronelle Landicho of Glasslake Funding claimed the Lender Underwriter of the Year award in the Specialist, Alternative and Private category for the second time, calling it a moment that never loses its impact.

"It's my second time winning, but it just never gets old. It feels like the first time," he said.

Landicho said the past year brought exceptional growth, with volume at Glasslake more than doubling year-over-year by his estimate. That’s a rise he attributed to his emphasis on building broker trust alongside technical underwriting skill. "I have a lot of deals that come in with brokers specifically asking me to underwrite their deals," he said. "People just think it's underwriting, but there's a lot of sales into it. You've got to sell yourself. You've got to build those relationships to gain the trust."

Laura Aiken, a senior underwriter at MCAP, won the Prime Lender Underwriter of the Year award with a broker-first approach and turnaround focus central to her success — especially in a year where rate competitiveness was not always assured.

"Even though our rates haven't always been there, know that my support is," she said. "I'm always just trying to get back to them as quickly as possible so that they know they'll have the best experience if they send their deals to us."

Cam Dellipizzi of MCAN Home Mortgage Group won Lender BDM of the Year in the Prime category and described the moment as a symbolic one for his career: he first attended the CMAs in 2012 as a Rookie of the Year winner, sitting at a table in the furthest corner of the venue from the stage.

"Tonight is like this full circle," he said. "I've done this job now since 2012 and I still don't get tired of working for the brokers."

He said his formula has not changed since then. "I pick up my phone, I answer my texts, I answer my emails. And I do pick up the phone at 5:00 on a Friday, and I take a lot of pride in that. It's all about relationship, being there for them when they need you."

Jerry Wieliczko of Hosper Mortgage was recognised as Lender BDM of the Year in the Specialist – Alternative and Private category after multiple nominations over the years.

"I'm very surprised. I never expected it," he said. "It was my eighth or ninth nomination, and finally I won." Wieliczko said his focus through a challenging housing market remained constant: "I'm always trying to help brokers wherever I can – to be wherever they need me."

Swish Goswami, CEO and co-founder of BrokerPlus, accepted the Industry Service Provider of the Year award for a company that had not yet reached its first anniversary — crediting the speed of the win to a philosophy built around listening to brokers.

"We started the company in March. It hasn't actually even been a year for us yet," said Goswami. "Some of the other companies in our space have forgotten sometimes that the brokers are really the people that you need to serve – and when I say serve, I don't just mean provide them something, I mean improve on it every day. Don't be satisfied by a product that you released in 2015 that was novel for its time."

Brokerages, teams, and networks

Clinton Wilkins of CENTUM Home Lenders in Halifax took home the Brokerage of the Year award for companies with fewer than 25 employees, bringing what he described as a point of regional pride back to Atlantic Canada.

"We have 10 brokers and the average broker on our team is doing over $50 million a year," said Wilkins. He attributed the team's success to a culture of education and client support: "Some of our secret sauce is really around education and really supporting our clients and our business partners — building a culture of success."

Wilkins also framed the win as a statement about his market. "Bringing the award home to Halifax and Atlantic Canada really puts us on the map and that we can compete with the big boys in Toronto and Vancouver."

Meaghan Hastings of The Mortgage Coach won the Brokerage/Team of the Year award for companies with 25 employees or more, crediting an investment in existing talent over new recruitment as the firm's key differentiator.

"We make a point of actually not focusing all of our efforts on recruitment," she said. "We really invest a lot in our agents and making sure that they are constantly improving, and hopefully that also improves us."

PMT Mortgage Corporation, led by Paul Meredith, was named New Brokerage of the Year. The team has operated for a decade but became an independent brokerage in 2024, Meredith said, making the award a significant milestone.

"It was hard not to get emotional up there," he said. "The biggest thing is that I've got a dream team that I put together." Meredith said the firm's success is rooted in a shared commitment to client experience. "We believe in building relationships with everybody, with all of our clients, and the entire team is right on board with that."

Dino DiPancrazio of M3 Financial Group accepted the Tru Cooperative Bank Award for National Brokerage of the Year on behalf of Mortgage Alliance, a multiple-time winner of the award. That’s a run he attributed to a broker-first philosophy and a growing investment in technology.

"Our motto for Mortgage Alliance is broker first always, and that is what we do," he said. "That's when the brokers need most support – in difficult times."

Rich Spence, president of Mortgage Centre Canada, accepted the National Broker Network of the Year award as a recognition of the more than 3,000 mortgage brokers his network represents across Canada.

"This really is for them," said Spence. "It's a network of individuals, entrepreneurs, lender partners, suppliers, and it's a great win for all of them." Spence said steady retention and ongoing recruitment underpin the network's growth.

Joel Wolodarsky and Shauna Clarke of IG Wealth Management accepted the Mortgage Industry Employer of Choice award for a firm that they said approaches mortgage advice through the lens of holistic financial planning.

"It takes building a star team because the mortgage business is really complex," said Wolodarsky. Clarke added that the firm's broader philosophy shapes the mortgage offering: "Our firm is focused on financial planning, and we provide mortgage advice in the context of a wider financial plan and reaching all of our clients' financial goals."

Innovation, community, and distinction

Dave Teixeira of DLCG won the Innovator Champion of the Year award, an honour he accepted as validation of a philosophy he has championed across the industry: build technology, then share it freely.

Among the tools Teixeira highlighted was an anti-money laundering risk rating tool released to the entire industry, which had seen more than 200,000 uses, according to Teixeira. "My overall philosophy on technology is it should be used to enhance lives, but then let's share it as far and wide as we can," he said. "In the age of AI, it's even easier to build – the barrier to entry is smaller, it democratises what we're doing."

Teixeira also spoke to the broader meaning of the category. "It's great to see that the industry is recognising that innovation is what's going to take us to the next step," he said. "How do we get from the industry that we've known to the industry that we could become?"

Dalia Barsoum, founder of Streetwise Mortgages/Streetwise Wealth, was named Finfluencer of the Year – a category introduced by REMIC recognising financial education delivered to Canadians through social media and digital channels.

Barsoum said her YouTube channel grew organically by responding to the questions her clients were raising. "With the market shift, people are having more and more questions about renewals, about private mortgages, about challenges we've never experienced before," she said. "I decided: I'm just going to talk about these things from a solution standpoint."

"For me, it's not about the clicks," Barsoum said. "It's really about putting out content that really makes a difference — content that informs, that people can remember and engage with. It just grew organically because what we're delivering, people saw value in."

Frances Hinojosa of Tribe was named Woman of Distinction, a recognition she described in terms of the generational shift she has witnessed over 30 years in finance.

"Thirty years ago, there were more suits in the boardroom than there were skirts," she said. "To be in finance and stick it out that long, to turn around and win the Women of Distinction – to me it's an honour to show the visibility to the next generation that it is possible for you to progress in anything that you want to do in your career moving forward."

Hinojosa offered advice for those starting out in their mortgage industry career: "Just keep going. Speak your mind. Be yourself. You think that you don't matter, but the little things will always matter the most in business."

Emily Kiparisas of SafeBridge Financial Group was named Young Achiever of the Year, an honour she described as "shocking" but deeply meaningful.

"I'm just really focusing on creating a different experience for a client and making them feel seen, recognised, understanding their life goals," said Kiparisas. She was quick to credit her team, describing them as integral to her work. "Without them, I wouldn't be where I am today."

Hugo Neveu and Jean-Francois Jacquet of CONSORTIUM Hypothécaire accepted the RFA Award for Excellence in Philanthropy and Community Service, dedicating the recognition to the causes – and the people behind them – that the firm supports.

The organisation has been a key backer of Strike Out Cancer, including helping to bring the initiative to Quebec City for the first time last year. "We try to do our best to support people in our community, especially children in need," the recipients said. "As an industry, we need to give back to everyone as soon as we can."

A milestone for the industry

Few awards at this year's ceremony carried as much weight as the Lifetime Achievement honour, presented to Jason Ellis of First National Financial LP – a recognition that also served as a fitting symbol for the CMAs' own 20-year journey.

"It's surreal, and I would say imposter syndrome taken to the next level," Ellis said. "I'm proud of a lot of what we accomplished together at First National, but I feel like I was just part of a team. Careers are built on teams. It's not really an individual thing."

Ellis acknowledged the individuals whose foundations he built upon: First National co-founders Stephen Smith and Maury Taws, and long-serving colleague Scott McKenzie. "I'm only here because of all of the people at First National. The sum of the parts much greater than the person."

Sponsors and closing

The evening was made possible by an impressive roster of sponsors: event partner the Coalition of Independent Mortgage Brokers of Canada (CIMBC), EQ Bank, Haventree Bank, Canadian Mortgages Inc. (CMI), MCAN, the Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC), Grechi Carter Professional Corporation, Real Property Solutions (RPS), RFA Financial, Tru Cooperative Bank, OIM Group, Bank of Montreal (BMO), HomeEquity Bank, and M3 Financial.

CMP extends its congratulations to all 25 category winners and its thanks to everyone who attended Wednesday night's celebration – and to all those who make the Canadian Mortgage Awards possible year after year.

items.title: GTA New Home Sales Post Best October In 3 Years As HST Rebate Deadline Nears
items.description:
New home sales in the Greater Toronto Area had their strongest October in three years, according to the Building Industry and Land Development Association (BILD).

There were 1,340 new home sales in October, up significantly from October 2025, according to Altus Group, BILD's official source for new home market data. That's still 51% below the 10-year average of 2,729 sales for the month.

BILD credits the HST rebate program, saying buyers are using the savings to shift toward more attainable homes like townhomes and stacked townhouses.

The expanded rebate removes the full 13% HST for eligible buyers of new homes priced up to $1 million, for a maximum rebate of $130,000. It runs until March 31, 2027.

Low-rise homes led the way. There were 958 low-rise sales in October, a significant increase from a year ago and 21% above the 10-year average. Low-rise includes detached, linked, and semi-detached houses and townhouses (excluding stacked townhouses).

High-rise homes, which include units in low-, medium-, and high-rise buildings and stacked townhouses, accounted for 382 sales, 80% below the 10-year average.

"GTA new home sales in October posted another strong showing thanks in large part to the HST rebate program. This month we saw the high-rise sector join the upswing with stacked townhouses hitting a nearly five-year high," said Edward Jegg, Research Manager at Altus Group. "Stacked townhouses offer more space than a condominium apartment and the HST rebate dramatically aids with the affordability crunch buyers are facing."

The benchmark price for a new low-rise home was $1,259,190, down 12.2% over the last 12 months. The benchmark price for a new high-rise unit was $1,053,085, up 2% from last year.

Both are gross prices that don't reflect the HST rebate. BILD reports them this way so they can be compared directly with previous years; buyers who qualify for the rebate would see additional savings.

Total remaining inventory in the GTA fell to 19,202 units. Low-rise inventory rose to 7,504 homes, or 11 months of inventory. High-rise inventory fell to 11,698 units, or about 44 months of inventory, based on average sales over the last 12 months.

In Simcoe County, there were 73 low-rise new home sales and no high-rise sales in October. The weighted average price of those low-rise homes was $968,212.

BILD is pushing the federal and provincial governments to extend the rebate before it expires.

"To date, there have been nearly 9,000 families in the province who have achieved new home ownership because of the HST rebate program. It also has supported nearly 34,000 industry jobs and stimulated $5 billion in economic activity and nearly $2 billion in provincial and municipal revenue," said Justin Sherwood, Chief Operating Officer at BILD.

"With the program set to expire on March 31, 2027, it would be incredibly impractical of the federal and provincial governments to not extend a program that is the sole bright spot of a very bleak housing picture."

items._ogDesc: Governor Tiff Macklem’s hawkish speech has BMO calling for a December rate hike to 2.75%, right as the Bank of Canada revives its old CPIX measure
items.body:
Canada’s central bank wasn’t discussing rate hikes, but it left a loud and clear message. Bank of Canada (BoC) Governor Tiff Macklem delivered a hawkish speech in Toronto this week, all but confirming rate hikes. BMO Capital Markets now expects the BoC to hike its key policy rate at its December meeting, after the Governor stated the economy no longer needs stimulus.

Bank of Canada Expected To Hike In December, Says BMO

After the latest comments from the BoC Governor, BMO sees a 25-basis-point hike in December. That would leave the policy rate at 2.75%, the mid-point of the neutral policy range, where monetary policy neither provides stimulus nor becomes restrictive. The hawkish tone appears to have surprised BMO, which noted the Governor didn’t address any economic weakness.

“Governor Macklem’s speech in Toronto reinforced the Bank of Canada’s recent hawkish messaging. He omitted any mention of the recent run of soft data, and reiterated worries about spillover from above-target headline inflation,” explains Benjamin Reitzes, BMO’s Canadian Rates & Macro Strategist. “One key rationale noted is that the economy no longer needs policy in stimulative territory.”

Bank of Canada Returns To Old Inflation Measure

Despite the finance industry taking away enough to update forecasts, the speech wasn’t meant to set expectations—at least not directly, notes BMO.

“The focus of the speech was the renewal of the inflation targeting framework, and the Governor unveiled that the Bank’s preferred core measures are now CPI-Trim and CPIX,” explains Reitzes.

Neither is a new core measure, but they’re not the headline numbers the media leads with. CPI-Trim seeks to strip out the extremes of the basket, eliminating the top and bottom 20% of price movements. It sounds like that would be a fair trade-off, but in reality, upward price pressure tends to be more extreme than downward. As a result, big price jumps are filtered out with much smaller relative moves downward.

The Governor clarified, however, that these measures will be used in addition to the headline CPI. “Mr. Macklem stressed that the 2% inflation target applies exclusively to headline CPI. The cores will be used as a guide to forecast where overall inflation is headed,” explains Reitzes.


As for CPIX, it stands for Consumer Price Index eXcluding, as it excludes the 8 most volatile components and the effects of indirect tax changes. It’s an oldie that was introduced in 2001, but dropped in 2016 in favour of three core measures—CPI-trim, CPI-median, and CPI-common. A good reminder that sometimes policymakers control inflation, and sometimes they control how it’s measured.

items.description: BMO projects 2% growth for Canada in 2027 as housing markets brace for further rate jumps
items.content: <p>BMO projects 2% growth for Canada in 2027 as housing markets brace for further rate jumps</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639312262342042131.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: BMO projects 2% growth for Canada in 2027 as housing markets brace for further rate jumps
items.body:
Canada's mortgage markets are heading into 2027 facing at least one more Bank of Canada rate hike, as BMO Capital Markets upgrades its national growth forecast to 2% while identifying British Columbia and Ontario as the provinces most exposed to continued monetary tightening.

The November 24 report by Douglas Porter, CFA, Managing Director and Chief Economist at BMO Capital Markets in Toronto, and Robert Kavcic, Director and Senior Economist at BMO Capital Markets, projects Canada's gross domestic product (GDP) above the 20-year average in 2027.

That follows an estimated 1% expansion in 2026, weighed down by US tariffs of 50% on steel and aluminum and 35% on lumber, with no significant trade resolution assumed in the base case.

"If we do get some kind of arrangement with the US, some certainty, some clarity on trade with the US, I would be much, much more optimistic in 2027, and I think we could grow well above average if we were to get some kind of an arrangement on trade," he said at the event.

On monetary policy, he was equally direct.

"We do believe that the Bank of Canada is likely to hike rates one more time," Porter said. "Our view is that two rate hikes will be enough."

Central banks globally raised rates this year as oil prices drove inflation higher, and Porter flagged that energy product prices — particularly diesel and heating oil — had not yet fully passed through to consumers.

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem already signalled the risk of a second-round oil shock and rising December rate odds.

The rate outlook is the most pressing near-term concern for mortgage professionals. Porter outlined the dual pressure on households in a March interview with Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"It's not good. On the one side, there's the hit to confidence because of the uncertainty for the outlook and the very real hit to people's pocketbooks from higher gasoline prices," he said.

"At the same time, we've had this backup in long-term bond yields, which is threatening to push up longer-term mortgage rates. It's tough for the housing market on both fronts."

Experts from the Bank of Canada, Dominion Lending Centres (DLC), and TD Economics say higher rates and inflation remain key factors shaping the outlook for borrowers and the mortgage market in 2027. https://t.co/SP0gdfkLH5 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 23, 2026

Ontario and BC most exposed to further rate hikes

The regional implications for mortgage professionals are significant. Kavcic identified British Columbia and Ontario as the provinces most vulnerable to continued tightening.

"Any upward pressure on mortgage rates would further deter buyers and slow construction activity, delaying a recovery in those markets," he noted in the report, citing elevated household debt and prolonged housing downturns in both provinces.

Ontario prices remain in retreat in some markets and construction has pulled back sharply; BC has endured a multi-year slump.

Regional divide deepens as prairies outperform

Alberta and Saskatchewan are delivering the country's strongest results, backed by elevated oil revenues and minimal US tariff exposure.

An influx of interprovincial residents has reinforced Alberta's consumer spending and residential demand.

Atlantic Canada is also above the national average, driven by migration and public infrastructure investment.

Quebec faces the steepest tariff headwinds, its aluminum sector absorbing a disproportionate share of US trade measures, compounded by its sensitivity to energy price volatility as a manufacturing base.

On the federal budget, Porter was clear about Ottawa's intent. 

"Their priority is really not on reducing the budget deficit — it is on supporting the Canadian economy through this difficult episode of trade uncertainty with the US," he said.

The projected $62.3 billion deficit for the 2026–2027 fiscal year arrives in line with expectations, and BMO estimates that defence and infrastructure commitments could add up to $150 billion to the economy over five years, with domestic suppliers prioritised.

items.description: High debt and rising delinquency signal growing strain for 2027 mortgage renewals
items.content: <p>High debt and rising delinquency signal growing strain for 2027 mortgage renewals</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639312227283291504.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: High debt and rising delinquency signal growing strain for 2027 mortgage renewals
items.body:
Canadian households entered the fourth quarter of 2026 carrying record consumer debt, with mounting pressure emerging among mortgage borrowers ahead of what is forecast to be a large renewal year in 2027, according to TransUnion Canada's Q3 2026 Credit Industry Insights Report (CIIR).

Total outstanding consumer credit debt reached $2.66 trillion in Q3 2026, up 3.8% year-over-year. The average Canadian owed $136,024 across all credit products, a 2.9% annual increase.

Mortgages represent 74% of outstanding balances, while non-mortgage debt – including credit cards, auto loans, and lines of credit – grew fastest at 3.6% year-over-year to an average of $28,083 per consumer.

Consumers in the super prime (lowest-risk) credit tier increased 4% year-over-year and represented nearly half of all scored credit-active Canadians.

Bigger balances, not more borrowers

Mortgage debt growth in Q3 2026 was not driven by an expanding pool of borrowers. Between September 2024 and September 2026, the average mortgage balance per consumer rose 8.6%, from $369,658 to $401,509, while the count of active mortgage holders grew by less than 1%.

While delinquency remains below pre-pandemic levels, the concentration of debt in larger individual balances is amplifying the financial stakes at renewal.

Matt Fabian, senior director of financial services research and consulting at TransUnion Canada, said lenders should closely track the divergence.

"Rising debt is being driven by two distinct forces: non-mortgage balance growth has come from an increase in borrowers carrying moderately higher average debt levels, while mortgage balance growth has come from larger balances per borrower as borrower counts have remained flat," Fabian said.

"For lenders, these differing patterns underscore the value of tracking how balances, product mix and payment obligations change over time."

Shaun Cathcart and Garry Bhaura of CREA, Michael Davenport of Oxford Economics, and Sherry Cooper of Dominion Lending Centres Group say higher rates and economic uncertainty are keeping Canada's housing market subdued. https://t.co/3C37E4W4gQ — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 18, 2026

Delinquency creep ahead of 2027 renewals

Mortgage delinquency trended upward across all stages in Q3 2026, with balance-level delinquency rising 6 basis points year-over-year and serious delinquency (90-plus days) outpacing account-level increases. That means larger-balance loans are overrepresented among distressed borrowers.

Victor Tran, Rates.ca mortgage and real estate expert, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year that mortgage arrears remain far from crisis territory.

"But I think it's going to be a slow grind," Tran said. "It's not going to be a significant, drastic increase suddenly and I don't think we're going to see sudden mass foreclosures or power of sales."

On October 28, the Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%, its first rate increase since July 2023, adding immediate upward pressure on adjustable-rate mortgages and complicating renewal calculations across a broad segment of the market. 

Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, said that financial pressure on homeowners is real even in the absence of a default crisis.

"Mortgage delinquency is often one of the last signs of financial strain, because most homeowners will cut back in other areas before missing a mortgage payment," she said.

"That's why even a small increase in arrears is worth paying attention to. It can suggest that some households have already used savings, leaned on credit, or reduced everyday spending to keep up. For borrowers coming up for renewal, the question isn't only whether they can make the next payment, but whether payments can be sustained over time."

Fabian added that warning signals typically surface elsewhere in a consumer's finances before a mortgage payment is skipped.

"Rising utilization, growing revolving balances, reduced payments and emerging delinquency on other products can signal weakening financial capacity before a mortgage payment is missed," he said.

"Having a comprehensive view across the consumer wallet can reveal early signs of mortgage stress and give lenders an opportunity to identify risk earlier and engage consumers proactively."

items.title: Bank of Canada: Experts’ 2027 expectations for the central bank
items.description: Here's what could be in store from the BoC over the next 12 months
items.content: <p>Here's what could be in store from the BoC over the next 12 months</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639312227730594328.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Here's what could be in store from the BoC over the next 12 months
items.body:
The Bank of Canada still has one interest rate decision to go before the end of this year – but with 2027 just around the corner, plenty of attention among mortgage shoppers and industry members is turning to the central bank’s likely approach to rates over the next 12 months.

The BoC’s 25-basis-point rate hike on October 28 was its first increase since July 2023, and with inflation expected to rise further as the US-Iran war continues, most experts say the central bank isn’t likely to announce a prolonged pause on rate jumps again anytime soon.

Each of the major Canadian banks is continuing to monitor the economic outlook closely as they map out the Bank of Canada’s possible rate path for 2027.

  • Bank of Montreal (BMO) sees a Q1 2027 move to 2.75%, with the bank moving its rate-hike call forward to the BoC’s next decision on December 9 following hawkish remarks by Governor Tiff Macklem this week.
  • Scotiabank expects gradual rate hikes by the central bank through 2027, with the Bank then set to hold at 3.25% through 2028.
  • Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) projects a rate hike in December, rising to 3.25% and remaining at that level through 2028.
  • Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) expects rates to hit 2.75% by March and remain at that level through 2028.
  • National Bank is expecting rates to reach 2.75% by the first quarter and 3% by the second. It sees rates remaining at that level until at least the end of 2028.
  • Toronto-Dominion Bank (TD) expects the Bank of Canada’s overnight target rate to hit 2.75% in Q1, remaining at that level for the rest of the year and through 2028.

Why rates are likely to keep rising

The main reason Canada’s banking giants see the central bank keeping rate hikes on the table is no secret: that Iran war has pushed up oil prices and sparked concern about the inflation outlook, with Macklem and other global central bank governors noting the potential for more price pressures spilling into 2027.

Five-year Government of Canada bond yields, which strongly influence fixed mortgage rates, moved steadily higher in August and September as financial market expectations hardened around BoC rate hikes.

In October, the Bank of Canada’s 25-basis-point rate increase was accompanied by remarks suggesting more hikes could be on the way, although decisionmakers struck a careful tone on the economic outlook.

“There could be a need to increase the policy rate further,” the Bank’s statement read, “but given uncertainties, Governing Council agreed to proceed carefully.”

This week, Macklem warned that energy cost pressures still haven’t fully reached consumers, keeping a BoC December rate hike firmly in play and hinting that the central bank is expecting inflation to remain sticky into 2027.

What the Bank of Canada’s rate path means for borrowers

While the Bank is back in rate-hiking mode, experts don’t see a flurry of rate hikes similar to those witnessed in 2022 and 2023, when the central bank tackled rampant inflation by spiking its benchmark rate by 475 basis points.

Instead, the increases are likely to be milder – but that will still have implications for Canadian borrowers. Variable-rate holders without a fixed payment will see their costs rise with each additional hike, and those with renewals due in 2027 could find themselves in a higher rate environment than when they last signed.

Fixed-rate borrowers aren’t shielded either. Their rates don’t rise and fall in line with BoC decisions, but those five-year Government of Canada bond yields are an important driver of fixed rates – and they often move in expectation of central bank rate changes.

Economists and experts are keen to emphasize that much will depend on how political and economic factors play out in 2027. The inflation picture and outcomes of the US-Iran conflict and ongoing Canada-US trade war will likely have much to say on the BoC’s approach to rates next year.

For now, all eyes are on December 9 and the Bank’s language in its statement, one which could give a clearer indication of how the central bank is weighing the outlook for the months ahead.
