items.description:
How much does Ottawa’s borrowing cost the rest of us, beyond what shows up in the budget? On Thursday, I testified before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance as part of its study on federal spending power. After I explained the implications of federal borrowing for credit markets, MP Michael Guglielmin pressed for […]

The post An MP Asked What Ottawa’s Borrowing Costs Canadians. Here’s the Math appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Federal borrowing could add 13 to 26 basis points to 5-year yields, costing mortgage holders $530 to $1,050 a year and governments billions more in interest.
items.body:
How much does Ottawa’s borrowing cost the rest of us, beyond what shows up in the budget? On Thursday, I testified before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance as part of its study on federal spending power. After I explained the implications of federal borrowing for credit markets, MP Michael Guglielmin pressed for an estimate. I didn’t have one, but it’s a good question, so I began modelling it as soon as I left the room. It’s even more than I assumed.

But first, let’s talk about how debt works.

How Government Borrowing Impacts What You Pay To Borrow

Credit is a market and, like any other, is priced on supply, demand, and risk. When there’s more capital than borrowers, rates fall as lenders compete for business. When borrowing outpaces the capital available, rates rise as borrowers compete for it. Riskier borrowers then pay a premium on top.

The lowest-risk borrower is the Government of Canada, which issues the currency. It pays the least, and its yield is the benchmark that everyone else’s borrowing is priced from. Someone like, I don’t know, Ricky from the Trailer Park Boys would pay the most because he fell behind on his vig.

When Ottawa borrows more, it pushes that benchmark up, and everyone pays more as well. Large businesses, small businesses, your car loan, your mortgage—they’re all priced off the same benchmarks. In finance, this is called crowding out.

Now back to the question. How much extra does this transmission cost, beyond the borrowing itself?

Households Could Pay Billions In Extra Mortgage Interest

We estimate the projected rise in federal market debt will add roughly 13 to 26 basis points to Canada’s 5-year bond yield. That means households can pay billions in extra interest per year once fully phased in, which isn’t exactly chump change. However, that’s just households—the burden extends to businesses and, ironically, the government’s own future financing. Here’s a high-level overview.

The most obvious hit would be to residential mortgages—about $3.2B to $6.3B in extra interest, or $190 to $380 per household per year. However, not all households have a mortgage—about 6 million do. That more realistically puts the burden at an average of $530 to $1,050 per year for those with a mortgage, and it would be concentrated among larger and more recent mortgages.

Applying the same transmission to all household credit puts the upper end at $4.3B to $8.7B per year. That averages about $260 to $520 for each of the 16.6 million households. That doesn’t include the growing use of private lenders, who tend to charge wider spreads as risk compensation.

We also estimate it would reduce borrowing power by roughly 1.3% to 2.6%. Interestingly, Bank of Canada (BoC) research on higher rates points to about the same decline in home prices over two years. If applied to the housing stock, that works out to roughly $111B to $222B in lost home equity. However, let’s stick to more direct costs, as modelling equity losses is a much deeper rabbit hole.

The drag on the housing industry is a more complex issue. While Ottawa’s borrowing is designed to stimulate certain aspects of building, it’s likely to hurt market-based outcomes. That doesn’t mean improved affordability either, since a large share is going towards large corporate landlords. Those are the same firms academics warn have outsized market power, raising rents much faster than mom-and-pop landlords. Another MP asked me about supply and affordability, and it deserves its own rundown next week.

Businesses Can Pay More—Unless They Have Ottawa’s Backing

Businesses face the same transmission. On corporate bonds alone, that’s roughly $1.2B to $2.4B per year in added interest. However, the bigger cost will be investments that no longer clear the higher hurdle rate. In my opening statement, I noted that Ottawa isn’t just providing big businesses with low-cost loans; it’s slanting the odds against the small and medium businesses that employ the majority of Canadian workers. This is part of the fallout: firms with Crown financing are shielded from the higher rate with taxpayer-subsidized loans, while everyone else faces higher costs.

The Irony: Ottawa’s Interest Bill Grows Too

One of the more interesting points is that this will also cost taxpayers. As federal debt is refinanced at higher yields, interest costs rise by roughly $3.1B to $6.2B a year once fully repriced. We use the 5-year yield as a proxy, since 10-year yields move more and T-bill rates less. The same transmission across federal, provincial and local debt works out to roughly $4.7B to $9.5B a year, ceteris paribus. That last part is a ten-dollar word for all else equal, and if you catch me using it in public, feel free to give me a firm slap.

There’s also a risk these estimates don’t capture—liquidity. As I noted in my opening statement, a growing share of Government of Canada bonds are absorbed by leveraged hedge funds. If that liquidity disappears, as it did in March 2020, the Bank of Canada has historically stepped in to buy—the same intervention that left it with roughly $10B in accumulated losses by the end of 2025.

Sounds like a banker’s wet dream, doesn’t it?

Our estimates use research from the CBO, Federal Reserve and Dallas Fed, which finds each point of debt-to-GDP adds 2 to 4 basis points to long-term yields. We scaled that to the 5-year yield using Bank of Canada research, then applied it to the rise in federal market debt projected in the government’s own debt and GDP forecasts. The figures are annual costs once fully phased in, using today’s debt balances, and each stands on its own rather than adding to the others. I’ll provide the committee with the full methodology in my brief, along with estimates for the questions that two other MPs raised.

items.title: In A Snap: Elevated Pre-Fab Has Landed In Vancouver
items.description:
A Vancouver homebuilder is making (very pretty) houses in a factory, and snapping them together on site in a matter of weeks.

Commonplace was founded in 2020 by architect Walker McKinley and partners Edmund Lee and Rich Frontain of McKinley Studios, a multi-pronged firm involved in architecture and interior design.

The idea was born out of a conversation McKinley had with friends over lunch. These recently-retired friends were building wood frame homes as hobby projects, and the conversation naturally turned to one question: why is home construction so broken? The linear, complex nature of traditional homebuilding means there’s no price or schedule certainty, and a senseless amount of materials are wasted throughout each project.

McKinley decided he wanted to change that. “We don't build cars the way we build homes, where every single one is a new prototype,” he says. “Why can't we build homes like we build cars?”

After years of research and development that included building prototype homes in warehouses and on farms to test new technologies and manufacturing systems, Commonplace successfully constructed its first home this May in Vancouver’s Mount Pleasant neighbourhood.

Standardized construction

The result is a highly standardized construction process, more akin to assembling an IKEA cabinet than what you imagine building a house looks like.

Lightweight polymerized cement and steel panels are built in a factory where excess waste is used to create more panels, rather than being disposed of. All elements are manufactured at the Squamish-based Nexii plant, North America’s first manufacturing facility to earn the TRUE (Total Resource Use and Efficiency) Gold Certification for Zero Waste.

After being shipped to site, the steel and cement exterior envelope panels are assembled. Inside, spaces are divided using standardized millwork or a pre-fab wall system. That prefab wall framing arrives precision-cut, with electrical junction boxes installed, clicking together on-site before finished surface panels are snapped on in place of drywall.

“We had a couple of rules: let's have no drywall, no trim and no saws,” says McKinley. “That means no cutting and measuring on site. Everything has to click into place.” All told, the Mount Pleasant home took four weeks to build, and the interior partition framing was installed in just one afternoon.

Because natural disasters are becoming a more serious threat in the region, McKinley also had the prefabricated parts be made non-combustible and flood-resistant.

View this post on Instagram
A post shared by McKinley Studios (@mckinleystudios)

Bespoke design

While standardization is often associated with cookie-cutter designs, Commonplace offers a range of home types and allows clients to customize colours, finishes, countertops, and other cosmetic details. Still, there is a cohesive look to the homes; one McKinley describes as “essential” rather than modern.

“We took a design ethos of ‘what do you really want in a home?’” he says. “To me that’s big windows, a courtyard that allows light and nature in and out of the home, a front porch that allows you to communicate with your neighbours and be part of a community, a big kitchen, lots of storage, and a beautiful architectural quality.”

Another key element of this essential design is to reduce unnecessary space like massive foyers and hallways, and utilize walls for additional storage. This includes two-feet deep storage spaces in many of the walls.

Currently, Commonplace offers a range of home types. This includes two-bedroom garden and laneway homes at 765 square feet, medium-sized bungalows, and two-storey homes ranging from 1,315 to 2,630 square feet, and larger versions ranging from 1,760 – 3,500 square feet.

Interest from diverse groups

While the builder only has one home under its belt so far, McKinley says they’re in the middle of placing an abundance of orders, and will be in full production in 2027.

A large portion of that interest has been from people who live in remote areas or on islands, where transporting materials and workers inflates construction prices. Because the homes are pre-fab, the kits can be efficiently transported, cutting down on both cost and emissions.

McKinley has also heard from developers who, facing low demand for condo towers, are turning towards single family pre-fab home communities. Their product has even caught the attention of resorts in Costa Rica and Hawaii, First Nations, and the military.

items.body:
Opening Statement before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance

Stephen Punwasi, Co-Founder and Chief Data Analyst, Better Dwelling.

Ottawa, November 19, 2026.

As prepared for delivery.

Thank you, Madam Chair, and members of the committee.

My name’s Stephen Punwasi, and my background is in behavioural finance and the levers that drive asset prices. I’m also the co-founder of Better Dwelling, Canada’s largest independent housing news outlet, where we focus on reducing information asymmetry.

Information asymmetry occurs when one party is better informed about a transaction than the other. This slants the odds in their favour, helping them to win. Since there’s no shortage of people willing to sing the praises—or fear mongering—over government spending, I’m going to do what we do at Better Dwelling and just explain the market dynamics and risk, hoping it reduces the asymmetry for all parties.

So let’s talk about borrowing, debt, and risks.

There are three things households and policymakers should understand about credit markets.

One: debt is future income, spent today, plus interest.

Borrowing for productive uses can pay for itself. The public is generally in agreement here, and the language Ottawa’s using resonates with that sentiment. However, an investment has to produce a return after its costs, including interest and opportunity costs.

Right now, Ottawa can’t tell us where the money is going. Roughly $260 billion is going to Crown Corporation loans and equity, and the budget doesn’t break down which ones get what. Housing is a good example. The PBO previously said it was unclear if the spending helped or just took credit for things that were happening. Since then, Ottawa ramped up the spending, building costs dropped, and fewer homes are being built. It costs less to build a home, the subsidies have climbed, and fewer are being built. That makes it pretty clear.

The bank grills me if I want to take my own money out for a used car. $260 billion is the equivalent of 16 million Canadian households going to work and paying taxes for a year, but Ottawa won’t tell the public where it’s going?

Two: The Price of Debt Depends On Who’s Borrowing

Debt is priced by supply, demand and risk. Ottawa borrows at the lowest rates in the country, since it runs the printing press. The issue is what happens next. Through its Crown corporations, it passes that cheap credit on to the projects it chooses.

Everyone outside those programs borrows at market rates. Small businesses can’t issue bonds, neither can households. They have to borrow from banks, and according to the latest lending conditions survey, face tighter conditions. Ottawa isn’t just borrowing, it’s helping big businesses succeed, while slanting the odds against the small and medium businesses that employ the majority of Canada’s workers. That’s a subsidy, and like any corporate handout, the public should know what it’s paying for.

Three: Know Your Lender & How Long They’ll Stay

Policymakers have been boasting of the foreign investment made in Canada, but they’ve been light on the details. Let me help with that. Almost zero of the net investment has been in equities. It’s all debt. Foreign investors absorbed all of Ottawa’s net new issuance in the first half of this year. This has created a tail risk that threatens the whole financial system, and I’m not just being hyperbolic. The Bank of Canada has quietly confirmed it.

Hedge funds account for over 40 percent of purchases at auctions, and typically fund those positions with overnight or short-term borrowing. They aren’t lenders the way a household thinks of one. They’re renting the bonds, on borrowed money, a day at a time.

The Bank of Canada warns that a funding disruption could force them to sell suddenly, calling it a “self-reinforcing liquidity spiral.” If I were advising a hedge fund today, I would tell them to make that play too.

During the last crisis, fiscal dominance forced the BoC to buy government bonds to provide liquidity. It was a big payday for investors; the BoC ended up with a $10 billion loss, the equivalent of 625,000 households’ federal taxes for a year.

It will happen again. A crisis for Canadians is a massive win for these foreign investors. Make no mistake, this play is a bet against Canada, not for it. This will be the difference between a recession and a financial crisis.

That backstop keeps Ottawa’s borrowing cheap today. The risk doesn’t go away. It moves to the public.

Is Ottawa making responsible investments for the future of Canada? I don’t know, and anyone who definitively says it is or isn’t is lying. Because Ottawa isn’t sure where the money is going either, it’s like the funds are allocated before anything is actually planned.

I’d ask the committee for three things. First, asset-level reporting for Crown lending and equity, including the subsidy built into below-market loans, so Parliament can see where the spending goes—and the public knows what their kids will be paying for. Second, outcome reporting for conditional transfers like housing. It’s simply not enough to spend money and take credit for wins and blame the economy for the losses. Third, reporting on who holds federal debt, how concentrated that base is, and how much of it is funded with short-term leverage, alongside each budget.

Banks and investors would ask those questions. Parliament—and the public—should be able to ask Ottawa them.

Thank you. I’m happy to take your questions.

items.body:
A partially-built residential high-rise building in Surrey’s City Centre, that is under a court-ordered sale, is back on the market.

Appearing to have found a buyer as it was listed this summer as being under contract, the project in the 13000-block of 101 Avenue is once again available, listed at $30 million.

“Construction on the project has progressed to the sixth floor above grade. Buyers can restart construction and benefit from over $23 million in hard costs spent to date, along with fully paid for entitlements and completed design drawings,” the listing by Goodman Commercial Inc. notes.

It had been marketed as “Centra,”an approved project comprising a 24-storey concrete tower and a two-storey townhouse and amenity building.

The project has 167 residential units above 194 stalls in two levels of underground parking.

The listing also notes, “Prior to construction delays, the project was successfully pre-sold; however, all contracts have since been rescinded, offering a new owner a clean slate to relaunch a sales program or reposition the asset as a market rental.”

Construction on the project ceased in August 2024 and Alvarez & Marsal Canada Inc. was appointed the receiver and manager earlier this year.

Home sales forecast to move up in Greater Vancouver next year

A new report by the British Columbia Real Estate Association (BCREA) forecasts home sales in Greater Vancouver going up, however, prices won’t correspond to that level of increase.

The BCREA’s 2026 Fourth Quarter Housing Forecast notes Multiple Listing Service (MLS) residential sales in BC are forecast to fall 4.5 per cent to 67,025 units this year.

The report notes that with active listings near their highest level since 2015, and additional pressure from elevated new-home inventory, the BCREA anticipates the average price in B.C. will fall by 1.2 per cent in 2026.

That decrease largely reflects disproportionate weakness in more expensive markets in the Lower Mainland, casting downward pressure on the broader provincial average price, the report explains.

In 2027, MLS residential sales are forecast to move higher, rising 7.2 per cent to 71,840 units.

Greater Vancouver is forecast to see an 8.7 per cent increase in 2027, after seeing decreases the previous two years.

The Fraser Valley is forecast to see an increase of 9.1 per cent.

The 2027 average MLS price is forecast to go up 2.2 per cent in Greater Vancouver and 1.8 per cent in the Fraser Valley.

“British Columbia’s housing market continues to face a challenging economic environment, as mounting headwinds fuel hesitancy among prospective buyers,” said BCREA Chief Economist Brendon Ogmundson in a news release. “Ultimately, we expect a modest recovery in home sales in 2027 as the impacts of new United States tariffs fade and fixed mortgage rates decline.”

items.title: Tracking Toronto’s 5 Tallest Rental, Condo Proposals (So Far) This Fall
items.description:
Toronto has never been shy about building up, and newsy developments like the Pinnacle towers and One Bloor West are proof that the high-rise fixation is alive and well.

But it’s not just the 80-storey-plus cohort that’s worth paying attention to. If you sift through the steady stream of development applications hitting the City’s desk, proposals in the the 40- to 60-storey range are impressive in their own rights, promising to add hundreds of new homes to the city while reshaping neighbourhood skylines.

Since September, there have been a handful of proposals that fit that bill, including a 56-storey rental that would displace the century-old City Morgue, a pair of 46-storey condos that have come out the other side of receivership, and a 61-storey condo slated for the burgeoning Etobicoke City Centre area. Here’s what's planned.

56 Storeys: 86 and 100-108 Lombard St and 103 Richmond St E

Rendering of 86 and 100-108 Lombard St and 103 Richmond St E/WZMH Architects

After initially proposing a 59-storey mixed-use building in 2022, Forum Asset Management and Slate Asset Management secured OLT approvals in 2025 for a much taller, 72-storey tower at 86 and 100-108 Lombard Street and 103 Richmond Street East — a parcel in Toronto’s Old Town area.

The most recent version of the proposal is considerably scaled back, describing a 56-storey mixed-use building (exclusive of a two-storey mechanical penthouse). The other major way the development departs from past plans is the unit tenure; while the 2022 proposal asked for 480 condo units, and the 2025 settlement was for 702 condo units, Forum and Slate are now planning 523 purpose-built rental units, alongside space for office and retail. The heritage-designated former City Morgue building at 86 Lombard Street would be relocated to the eastern portion of the development site to make way for the proposed.

Learn more.

50 Storeys & 50 Storeys: 60 Overlea Blvd

Rendering of 60 Overlea Blvd/Sweeny&Co Architects

The Ontario Line is inching towards the finish line, and 60 Overlea Boulevard in Thorncliffe Park — currently occupied by an under-utilized retail plaza — is one of the many Toronto addresses that will benefit from the forthcoming transit connectivity. The site is less than 500 metres from the future Thorncliffe Park station, and a proposal from landowner Plazaworks Inc. describes a pair of 50-storey towers with a shared podium. All 1,261 units would be rental in tenure, while the ground floor would be reserved for non-residential uses, including a potential childcare facility.

Plazaworks is also seeking official plan and zoning bylaw amendments to re-designate the property from General Employment Areas to Mixed Use Areas, which would pave the way for some of the proposed non-residential space to be used for “employment-generating uses.”

Learn more.

46 Storeys & 46 Storeys: 7 Labatt Ave And 77 River St

Rendering of 7 Labatt Ave and 77 River St/Giannone Petricone Associates

A long-stalled development site at 7 Labatt Avenue and 77 River Street — on the edge of Regent Park, about a kilometre from the future Corktown station of the Ontario Line — is now under the ownership of KingSett Capital, with the firm now planning a pair of 46-storey towers. The high-rises would have 1,170 condo units between them, while a separate two-storey Salvation Army building is planned to the east (replacing the Salvation Army building currently at 7 Labatt). The plans also include a publicly accessible open space running between the 46-storey towers.

The site was initially being redeveloped by TAS in favour of their “Labatt Village” project, set to include 48- and 44-storey buildings with 1,240 units. The project was placed under receivership in February, and KingSett took over through an $84.15-million credit bid this summer, paving the way for the site’s next chapter.

Learn more.

50 Storeys: 4632-4648 Yonge St and 16-18 Cameron Ave

Rendering of 4632-4648 Yonge St and 16-18 Cameron Ave/Arcadis

While some developments hinge on the forthcoming Ontario Line, others make use of the transit Toronto already has. A proposal from Yonge and Cameron LP is for a 50-storey mixed-use tower at 4632–4648 Yonge Street and 16–18 Cameron Avenue in North York, where it would replace a two-storey commercial plaza and two detached houses around 200 metres from the Sheppard-Yonge subway station. The site is also within the North York Centre and a designated Protected Major Transit Station Area, where the City is encouraging further intensification.

The development would introduce 569 new residential units to the site — all condo in tenure — and the continued operation of the existing autobody shop at 4656 Yonge. The tower would also include ground-floor retail and indoor and outdoor amenity spaces designed with families with children and pet owners in mind.

Learn more.

61 Storeys: 1234 Islington Ave

Rendering of 1234 Islington Ave/Sweeny&Co Architects

After securing City Council approvals in June, Montez Corporation has moved ahead with site plan control application for a 61-storey mixed-use tower at 1243 Islington Avenue in central Etobicoke, where it would replace a 12-storey office building. Though the City approved 702 condo units and a retail component for the site, the latest planning documents show that the unit-count has been cut down to 527. In addition, it seems the project has been switched to purpose-built rental, and 16 units are planned to be affordable.

The site is less than 200 metres from Islington Station, within a Protected Major Transit Station Area, and leans into a wider push to reshape the neighbourhood into a more complete community. Nearby, the new Etobicoke Civic Centre is coming up on what’s locally known as the Westwood Theatre Lands, where it will accommodate a new library, recreation centre, child-care centre, public health clinic, and civic square.

items.title: Housing minister won't reaffirm Liberal pledge to double home construction
items.description: OTTAWA — Housing Minister Gregor Robertson wouldn't reaffirm the Liberal government's long-standing goal of doubling the pace of home building when pressed by reporters on Wednesday.
items._ogDesc: OTTAWA — Housing Minister Gregor Robertson wouldn't reaffirm the Liberal government's long-standing goal of doubling the pace of home building when pressed by reporters on Wednesday.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Housing Minister Gregor Robertson wouldn't reaffirm the Liberal government's long-standing goal of doubling the pace of home building when pressed by reporters on Wednesday.

The Liberals campaigned during the 2025 election on a pledge to double the annual pace of housing starts to roughly 500,000 over a decade.

But that promise was absent from the federal budget tabled on Nov. 5. The Liberal government instead set new goals in Budget 2026 to triple the pace of non-market housing construction over the next decade and to end homelessness.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan noted the missing reference to doubling home construction in a series of reports analyzing the budget published Tuesday.

"While Budget 2026 announces new measures for homelessness and housing affordability, it is not on track to double housing starts per Budget 2025, with year-to-date housing starts 4 per cent lower in 2026 than 2025," one of Ryan's report read.

The Canadian Press asked Robertson's office last week whether the Liberals were sticking to the target. A spokesperson for his office pointed to a statement sent to The Canadian Press six months earlier reaffirming the pledge.

Reporters asked Robertson as he was heading into the Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday if the government is sticking to the pledge it campaigned on a year and a half ago.

"We're just focused on supply overall for the time being. Affordable supply first and foremost," he said in response.

Robertson said the goal of doubling housing starts was based on the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp.'s estimates of the supply gap, or the number of homes the country needed to add to restore affordability to 2019 levels.

Hitting that annual pace requires the private sector to build at scale, he said, adding the government is "doing everything" it can to stabilize markets like Toronto and Vancouver that are struggling to get shovels in the ground.

The minister said the government has made "unprecedented" interventions to stimulate construction, including moves to axe the GST on many newly built units and other federal incentives to get municipalities to lower costly development charges.

But "the Government of Canada cannot force Canadians to build housing," he said.

"Right now we're doing everything that we can in a very challenging time for our economy," Robertson said.

"We have to continue focusing on where we intervene, working with provinces and cities to get them building as much as possible and looking at the affordable side. That's where the role of government is, to make sure there's affordable housing getting built."

Non-market housing is usually more affordable and relies on government support to get built — but those homes account for only a small share of the overall number of units built in a year.

Conservative housing critic Scott Aitchison accused the Liberals of quietly dropping their homebuilding target and moving the goalposts.

"Their big promises have become another Liberal housing illusion. Tripling the speed of slow is still unbearably slow and will not make homes affordable again," he said in a media statement on Tuesday.

In its fall housing supply report, the CMHC wrote that the country is entering a "new phase" where slowing population growth is leading to more balance in Canadian rental markets.

But the Crown corporation warned that the annual pace of housing starts is well short of levels needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability to the market in the next 10 years.

The CMHC's "business-as-usual" forecast sees Canada breaking ground on 231,000 homes per year, which it estimates would leave the market up to 238,000 homes short of affordable levels by 2036.

Affordability will remain out of reach if Canada fails to take advantage of this moment to rapidly build housing supply ahead of the next surge in demand, the CMHC said.

Experts point out that many of the levers to increase housing supply are outside the government's direct control, such as Bank of Canada interest rates and the cost of building materials.

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Institute, told The Canadian Press last week that he never liked the goal of doubling housing starts because it could be "excessive" and lacks a nuanced approach to the mix of homes Canada must build.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

The post Canadian Real Estate Prices Not Expected To Rise Through 2030: BMO appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: The Canadian real estate correction is already the largest in history, and gets even bigger after inflation. It's not over, according to BMO.
items.body:
Canadian real estate’s historic price correction is slowing down, but the pain may not be over. In a research note to investors, BMO Capital Markets explains it’s even larger in real terms. The banks warn that the math doesn’t work out in favour of households, who are still struggling with affordability. Combined with the recent upward pressure on interest rates, they see real home prices falling further for at least another year.

Canadian Home Price Declines Slowing After Historic Drop

The historic correction for Canadian home prices isn’t over, but it is losing steam. Price declines are getting smaller, with another bank even declaring the bottom. “Canadian home prices appear to be nearly flattening out in nominal terms, but the adjustment is ongoing after accounting for inflation—and we suspect it will continue,” says BMO Economist Robert Kavcic.

The latest national benchmark from CREA shows a typical home has shed 22.8% (-$191.6k) from the March 2022 peak. In the past year, the benchmark fell 3.1% (-$20.7k), a relatively small move in contrast to the $649.9k benchmark. However, those declines are in nominal terms. In real (inflation-adjusted) terms, the market is a whole different story.

Canadians Have Seen Inflation Run Hot—and It’s Not Slowing Down

October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) report shows prices are 3.1% higher than last year, over 50% higher than the BoC target. Consumer prices have grown 19.9% from 2020 to 2025, or 3.7% annualized over the 5 years. Significantly outpacing the target inflation rate means stronger depreciation in real terms.

“Real Canadian home prices are down 4.7% from a year ago after inflation, and are now down a massive 20% from five years ago— that’s the steepest five-year real decline on record going back to the start of the 1980s,” notes Kavcic.

Canadian Home Prices Not Expected To Rise Through 2030

Inflation-adjusted average Canadian home price.

Source: BMO Capital Markets; CREA.

One may assume the sharpest drop in history means the market is ready to return? Not exactly.

“Given where valuations still sit relative to income and rent, and assuming that interest rates are nudging higher rather than headed lower, there is simply no scope for price increases to run ahead of inflation at this stage,” warns Kavcic.

He’s not outright dismissing the possibility of an uptick in home prices. The math is just working against it, especially when it comes to real terms.

“Thus, even if nominal prices turn the corner, the adjustment relative to inflation (and, similarly, relative to household income) will continue in the year (or more) ahead,” warns Kavcic.

items.title: Choice Properties REIT Buys Royal Oak Wholesale Club In Burnaby For $38.5M
items.description:
Toronto-based Choice Properties REIT (TSX: CHP.UN) has acquired a Wholesale Club at a prominent intersection in Burnaby, British Columbia, and the site is primed for redevelopment.

The Wholesale is located at 5335 Kingsway near the intersection with Royal Oak Avenue in the Royal Oak neighbourhood, a few blocks north from the Expo Line SkyTrain’s Royal Oak Station.

The 2.84-acre property is occupied by a Wholesale Club, a Costco-like chain owned by Loblaw Companies Limited, which is in turn owned by George Weston Limited.

On September 8, Choice Properties REIT acquired 5335 Kingsway for $38,500,000, according to the REIT’s Q3 2026 report published last week. The transaction closed for a total of $39,731,000 when including related costs. The vendor was Arbutus Properties Ltd.

BC Assessment values 5335 Kingsway at $40,153,000 in its latest assessment, which is dated to July 1, 2025.

Loblaw Companies is the largest unitholder in Choice Properties REIT and also one of its major tenants.

The acquisition represents the largest acquisition the REIT has made in 2026, and Loblaw now represents 57.1% of the REIT’s rental revenue.

The Property

The 5335 Kingsway property has been on the market for over a year now, after being listed for sale last summer by Kevin Douglas, Edgar Buksevics, Kevin Meikle, and Colton Zayshley of JLL on an unpriced basis.

Last spring, the City of Burnaby approved the Royal Oak Community Plan, laying the groundwork for the neighbourhood to be redeveloped, with the intersection of Royal Oak Avenue and Kingsway being identified as the key “Village Centre Node.”

The Village Centre Node consists of only a few properties at the northeast corner of the intersection, one of which is 5335 Kingsway. Under the Royal Oak Community Plan, the site can accommodate high-rise development up to 30 storeys.

A preliminary conceptual development for 5335 Kingsway in Burnaby. (Arcadis, JLL)

The property was marketed by JLL with that development potential in mind, with JLL saying in their sales brochure that “the property’s size accommodates various development options including multiple towers, retail space, and diverse amenities.”

“An additional 10 storeys are available through the City of Burnaby’s Community Benefit Bonus Policy, increasing potential heights up to maximum of 40 storeys,” JLL added. “Conceptual plans for 5335 Kingsway envision 1,028,463 sf of developable area and 8.32 FSR under the base 30 storey zoning, across a 3 tower mixed-use built form.”

The real estate market is still amidst a downturn, but the Wholesale Club — the building being 47,775 sq. ft — “provides consistent interim holding income to the Property while developers work through entitlements and development vision.”

Choice Properties REIT

Although its primary focus is retail, Choice Properties REIT is also a developer now that large retail properties have become prime for intensification.

Over in Coquitlam, at the boundary with Burnaby, Choice Properties REIT has partnered with Vancouver-based developer Wesgroup to redevelop 439 and 465 North Road — a Denny’s and the Cariboo Centre retail plaza — into a master-planned community with six high-rise towers, as previously reported by STOREYS.

Earlier this year, Choice Properties REIT partnered with Toronto-based private equity real estate investment firm KingSett Capital to acquire First Capital REIT (TSX: FCR.UN) in a $9.4 billion deal.

According to Choice’s Q3 report, both First Capital REIT’s unitholders and the Ontario Superior Court gave their stamp of approval for the deal in June and the transaction is expected to close in Q4 2026 or Q1 2027.

As for Q3, the REIT reported that their occupancy rate was 91.4% for mixed-use and residential properties, 97.5% for retail properties, and 98.6% for industrial properties. Funds From Operations (FFO) per unit diluted grew by 2.2% year over year and is now $0.284 while same-asset net operating income grew by 3.1%.

items.title: AI answers the call for B.C.'s real estate industry
items.description: Realtors in B.C. and beyond turn to AI to reach clients, streamline their work
items._ogDesc: Realtors in B.C. and beyond turn to AI to reach clients, streamline their work
items.body:
Han Lee says making and answering client calls is one of his biggest challenges as a Realtor, often leaving little time for himself and his family.

So he and his business partners built an AI receptionist that’s on call 24 hours a day.

Their software uses AI to answer incoming phone calls and take down clients’ information and requests. Initially built for his own business, the system is now being offered to other real estate companies.

“As a one-person Realtor or a one-person owner of the business, there's only so much you can do,” said Burnaby-based Lee, owner of the JulyWork administrative software tool.

The system connects to the company’s calendar and can book appointments with Realtors based on their availability, areas of expertise and language skills, according to Lee.

“Our ‘receptionist’ … can pick up to 100 calls at a time,” he said, adding that the team developed it so the voice sounds like a real person.

Lee said AI can also identify highly specific property features that would otherwise require Realtors to manually review individual listings and photographs.

“It is so smart that it can search very weird and sophisticated things that people will never be able to really do,” he said.

Human connection hard to replace

Mike Stewart, a Vancouver-based Realtor and real estate blogger, said AI has become increasingly integrated into his work over the past few years, particularly for writing property listings, creating marketing content and conducting research.

However, he sees AI as most useful for time-consuming administrative and back-end tasks, allowing Realtors to focus on the most important part of their job — connecting with clients.

“And so then time is freed up for the Realtor to spend more time generating business by speaking to people or following up with past clients to strengthen the relationships,” he said.

While AI can identify properties that match a buyer’s stated requirements, Stewart said it cannot always anticipate a client’s potential needs in the same way an experienced Realtor can.

“We're dealing with human nature, and so often the journey of buying a property often takes a path that is not predictable initially,” said Stewart.

For example, a client who originally wants a two-level red house may end up buying a four-storey blue house, he said.

“So much of what we do is helping the clients understand how a house may work for their lives and supporting them with that,” said Stewart.

“And it's very much a subjective feel type of thing where the people go into the house, they see it and they feel it. And there's limits to what an artificial intelligence can do to help them with the feel.”

Marketing content shows up in AI search

As more buyers turn to AI platforms to search for properties and real estate services, companies should pay greater attention to the content they publish online to improve their visibility in AI-generated answers, according to Gerardo Bonilla, co-founder and CEO at Temso AI.

His marketing firm, which helps businesses improve their visibility in AI-generated search results, analyzed around 80,000 source citations for the luxury real estate industry and released a report in October.

One of the main findings was that Google AI Mode drew about 83 per cent of their citations from commercial websites, said Bonilla. The report found similar results across other AI platforms, including 77 per cent for Google AI Overviews, 80 per cent for Gemini and 79 per cent for ChatGPT.

“That [means] most of the sources in the way that [AI] weighs who to trust when it comes to answering these questions come from commercial websites,” said Bonilla.

“What that means specifically for brands is that in this industry, their content on their website matters a lot.”

Those sources can include real estate agencies publishing their own content, as well as resellers and comparison websites, he added.

Although the algorithms behind AI-generated answers remain difficult to understand fully, Bonilla said real estate companies can take steps to improve the likelihood that their websites will be cited.

These include ensuring AI citation bots can access their websites, and publishing content in a format that makes it easier for AI systems to identify and reference relevant information.

“For example, AI citation bots love primary data. So if there's any primary data that you have, then you can be publishing,” he said.

He also recommended that companies write in a way that they're answering the question in full in a very specific way.

“So humans, we tend to be able to ‘read between the lines,’ whereas AI citation bots prefer writing that is a lot more explicit,” said Bonilla.

“So the more explicit you are and the more in-depth you answer a certain topic, the likelier you are to basically get picked up by an agent.”

items._ogDesc: October home sales crept up slightly from the previous month but were still down more than 10 per cent from a year ago, the Canadian Real Estate Association said in its latest report Tuesday. Home sales last month totalled 37,827, down 10.
items.body:
October home sales crept up slightly from the previous month but were still down more than 10 per cent from a year ago, the Canadian Real Estate Association said in its latest report Tuesday.

Home sales last month totalled 37,827, down 10.6 per cent from October 2025. But on a seasonally adjusted basis, activity edged up 0.3 per cent compared with September.

“Despite most forecasters sharpening their pencils and lowering their predictions, so far we’ve only seen a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, probably less than many would have predicted in an environment of rising interest rates,” Garry Bhaura, CREA's chair, said in a news release.

“With the market moving into its traditionally quieter months, now is a great time to shift into planning mode for 2027."

The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month — the first hike in more than three years — to reduce the risk that stubbornly high oil prices become persistent inflation.

The move prompted Canada's big banks to raise their benchmark prime rates, pushing the amount charged on variable rate mortgages higher.

A summary of deliberations released earlier this month by the central bank also suggested its governing council thinks it might need to raise rates further, but will proceed carefully.

Michael Davenport, senior economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a report Tuesday that Canada's resale housing market had a quiet October and is heading into "hibernation" for the winter.

"Rising mortgage rates, a soft labour market and elevated job insecurity from the trade war with the United States will likely cause housing demand to weaken in the near term, pushing home sales and prices modestly lower before a tepid recovery gets underway next spring," he wrote.

"We don’t expect the recent softness in the housing market to deter the (Bank of Canada) from hiking ... to 2.75 per cent in December."

Meanwhile, CREA said the national average sale price in October ticked down 1.6 per cent from a year ago to $678,584.

New listings fell 5.5 per cent to 75,814, but on a seasonally adjusted basis, were up 0.8 per cent from the month before and outpaced sales activity.

CREA said there were about 197,000 properties listed for sale on all Canadian MLS systems at the end of October, up slightly from the long-term average of 190,000.

It said there were five months of inventory on a national basis at the end of October, up slightly from the summer.

Cailey Heaps, CEO at Heaps Estrin Real Estate Team in Toronto, said deals are coming together when sellers have realistic expectations about pricing and buyers are willing to act.

The segment that's been the most challenging has been for properties that are "family homes" to be lived in long-term.

"Those people are currently housed, so they don't feel any pressure to act. They want to take a bit of a wait-and-see approach," she said.

"The first-time buyer market is very active — incredibly active."

Heaps is expecting a "fairly flat" market through the winter as concern over job security and tariffs weigh on confidence.

"And then I do think that spring will start to see an uptick, not only in pricing but also in volume."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate’s has one of the largest corrections in history and it’s still going, as buyers balked at this price level in October.
items.body:
Canadian real estate has made one of the sharpest corrections on record, and it’s still going. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows prices fell further in October. Weak demand and lofty inventory suggest that buyers are still balking at this level. Over 4 years in a correction have only rolled back 13 months of 2020’s low rate, speculative boom.

Canada’s Housing Correction Reversed 13 Months of Gains

The price of a typical home across Canada.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home slipped 0.3% (-$2.1k) to $649.9k in October, 3.1% (-$20.7k) lower than last year. Prices are now 22.8% (-$191.6k) lower than the March 2022 peak, and sit just a little higher than they were back in February 2021. Nearly half a decade of correcting, and most Canadians still couldn’t afford to buy, even if they wanted to.

Canadian Home Sales Fall, Remain Historically Weak

Canadian home sales on the MLS in October.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

There was an abrupt drop in home sales last month. Only 37.8k homes were sold in October, 10.6% fewer than last year and marks a 3-year low. That doesn’t sound bad, but excluding the slowdown since 2022, this level was last seen in 2012. Home sales are better than they were at the start of the downturn, but are still hovering around levels seen in the wake of the global financial crisis.

Canadian Home Sellers Still Flooding The Market

New listings of homes for sale on the Canadian MLS, October.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The inventory side weakened too—just not as much as it did when it comes to home sales. CREA reported 75.8k new listings in October, 5.5% lower than last year, and just a smidge under October 2024. This may be a 3-year low, but October’s new listings have never been this strong before 2020.

A sharper drop in sales left the sales-to-new-listings ratio (SNLR) at 49.9% in October, 2.8 points below last year. The ratio is technically in balanced territory, but this time of year tends to see sellers pull back. The SNLR doesn’t show a buyer’s market, but October hasn’t seen the ratio this low since 2008. In fact, that’s the only October to come in lower in the past three decades.

When does this market downturn end? This is one of the sharpest downturns on record, yet not much progress has been made. The market’s been like a slow-moving car crash, spending over 4 years rolling back just 13 months of gains. Home prices in Canada have always moved fast, but from 2015 to 2022 was another story. Taxpayer-backed incentives helped to grow prices much faster than incomes and credit capacity. The inefficiencies didn’t build up overnight, and they won’t correct overnight either.

items.title: Canadian Home Sales Inch Up In October As Interest Rates Climb
items.description:
The Canadian housing market barely moved in October, which is a better result than many forecasters expected heading into fall. Home sales on Canadian MLS® Systems rose 0.3% from September, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA).

October also brought a rate hike from the Bank of Canada. CREA doesn’t expect it to turn into a repeat of 2022.

“In a widely expected move, the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate at its October 28 announcement with the goal of tamping down Canadians’ concerns about creeping inflation stemming from higher energy costs,” said Shaun Cathcart, CREA’s Senior Economist. “That said, with the Bank’s preferred inflation measures still very well behaved, this is unlikely to be a repeat of the 2022 tightening cycle. Rather, it is more likely to be of the mild to moderate variety, although that distinction does carry extra weight in times of stretched affordability.”

So far, buyers haven’t pulled back much. “Despite most forecasters sharpening their pencils and lowering their predictions, so far we’ve only seen a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, probably less than many would have predicted in an environment of rising interest rates,” said Garry Bhaura, CREA Chair.

The year-over-year comparison is weaker. Actual (not seasonally adjusted) sales were 10.6% lower than in October 2025.

New listings grew 0.8% month-over-month. Listings rose a little faster than sales did, so the national sales-to-new listings ratio slipped to 48.7% from 49% in September. That’s under the long-term average of 54.7%, but still within the 45% to 65% band CREA associates with a balanced market.

There were roughly 197,000 properties listed for sale nationwide at the end of October, slightly above the long-term average of 190,000. At this point in the year, inventory has ranged from 100,000 listings in fall 2021, when the COVID-19 housing boom was at its peak, to 250,000 a little over a decade ago.

Measured in time, the market had five months of inventory at the end of October. That’s up slightly from the summer and exactly in line with the long-term average. By CREA’s measure, a seller’s market sits below 3.6 months and a buyer’s market sits above 6.4 months.

On prices, the National Composite MLS® Home Price Index (HPI) rose 0.1% from September. CREA said that gain could reasonably be called flat, or the biggest monthly increase in two years.

On an annual basis, the non-seasonally adjusted HPI was 3.1% below October 2025. That’s a smaller drop than September’s and smaller than most of the readings so far in 2026.

The non-seasonally adjusted national average home price came in at $678,584, which is 1.6% lower than a year earlier.

The slow season is next. “With the market moving into its traditionally quieter months, now is a great time to shift into planning mode for 2027,” said Bhaura.

CREA will release its next set of statistics on Tuesday, December 15, 2026.

items.title: Insider: Ontario And Quebec Are Running Opposite Housing Experiments
items.description:
I have lost count of how many times I have heard that Toronto and Vancouver are a special case. Too expensive, too much debt, a local hangover. October is getting in the way of that story.

In CREA's residential numbers, Greater Toronto sales were down 7.9% from last October. Greater Vancouver was down 10.7%. Calgary was down 12.8%. Ottawa was down 10.8%. Montreal was down 17.6%. The country was down 10.6%. If those two cities were still a quarantine zone, the others would not be on that list.

Prices have not followed in every market, and that is the part worth sitting with. Calgary's benchmark was unchanged at $569,300. Montreal's was still up 1.4%, to $591,400. Ottawa was only down 1.5%. Toronto is down 4.4% on the year and 13.7% over three years. Vancouver is down 5.2%. Volume goes first. Price lags. Then the "isolated incident" starts to look like a leading indicator.

Two provinces, opposite directions

That national demand story sits on top of a supply split I still think is the more interesting chart in this release. Ontario recorded 33,510 new residential listings in October, 8.8% fewer than a year ago, against 14,053 sales, down 8.7%. Quebec went the other way on supply: 13,864 new listings, up 6.2%, against 7,451 sales, down 12.6%. Ontario's new listings have run below year-ago levels for essentially all of 2026. Quebec's have run above.

Chart: New listings, year-over-year %, Ontario vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

The Greater Toronto benchmark is $928,800, down 4.4% year over year. Mississauga is down 8.5%. Quebec CMA is up 5.1%, and 33.6% over three years. Ontario is tightening the shelf and still losing price. Quebec is adding listings and still gaining some.

Toronto tightened by subtraction

Through the first ten months of 2026, the Greater Toronto Area logged 145,345 new listings, 14.7% fewer than the same period last year. Sales were 52,694, down only 1.8%. The year-to-date sales-to-new-listings ratio rose to 36.3% from 31.5%.

That "improvement" came from sellers stepping back. Buyers did not arrive. Even after a year of withdrawals, Toronto's seasonally adjusted ratio was 39.1% in October, still under the 45% floor of CREA's balanced range.

Chart: Sales-to-new-listings ratio, seasonally adjusted. Toronto vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

Montreal moved the other way. Year-to-date new listings rose 6.3% to 69,458 while sales fell 8.7% to 37,091, pulling the ratio down to 53.4% from 62.2%. Montreal is loosening from a seller's market toward balance. Toronto is crawling up from a buyer's market by shrinking the choice set.

Chart: Months of inventory, seasonally adjusted. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

I would not tell a Quebec builder the Ontario correction has landed in Montreal prices. I also would not tell them demand is insulated. Montreal sales were down 17.6% in October, in a market where prices are still rising. Some of that is rates. Montreal's benchmark sits about $337,000 below Toronto's, so a hike bites less than it does on a GTA loan. Some of it, in my view, is confidence and equity travelling. When Toronto and Vancouver values fall, owners feel poorer. They spend less and they move less. Investors who hold product in more than one city get careful. Lenders do too. I cannot show you a contagion index. I can show you volumes weakening in places that were supposed to be fine.

The pipeline tells the longer story

Resale listings are this month's supply. Housing starts are the supply of 2029 and 2030.

From January through September 2026, Ontario's housing starts averaged a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 61,200, according to CMHC data compiled on Homies stats. Quebec averaged about 60,100. Ontario's pace is down 5.7% from the same months of 2025. Quebec's is up 1.8%.

Those two numbers are nearly identical. The provinces are not. Statistics Canada estimates Ontario's population at about 16.26 million and Quebec's at about 9.07 million as of July 2026. Per 1,000 residents, Quebec is starting homes at an annualized pace of roughly 6.6. Ontario is at roughly 3.8.

Chart: Housing starts, seasonally adjusted annual rate, Ontario vs Quebec, indexed to January 2022. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CMHC via Statistics Canada.

Ontario's resale market is reaching balance by holding product back. Its development pipeline is doing the same thing. If the demand softness in Toronto is a leading indicator rather than a local mess, that is a problem for anyone underwriting 2028 absorption in the rest of the country.

The condo collapse is a resale problem first

Nationally, condo starts from January through September totalled 25,719, down 34.8% from 39,446 in the same months of 2025. Purpose-built rental starts rose 8.6% to 90,623.

Chart: Condo vs rental housing starts, Canada, indexed to January 2023. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CMHC via Statistics Canada.

Presale condo projects need buyers willing to pay tomorrow's price today, and lenders need those presales before construction financing flows. When the GTA resale benchmark is down 13.7% over three years, the comparable undercuts the presale, the presales do not get sold, and the project does not start.

A rate hike makes that worse. The Bank of Canada raised the overnight rate to 2.50% from 2.25% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023. Then the five-year Canada bond, the thing lenders actually price a fixed mortgage off, jumped from 3.33% to 3.60% in under a week, as Robert McLister noted in the Financial Post on November 16. Buying power got tighter after the October deals were already written.

Confidence was not exactly roaring into that. The Bloomberg-Nanos Canadian Confidence Index was 50.98 for the four weeks ending October 30, below its long-term average of 54.65. The expectations index, which includes the outlook for the economy and property prices, sat at 47.77. Nik Nanos called it the slow lane. A presale buyer is being asked to commit years out, with their home equity worth less and their fixed rate already moving. Rental is holding up because its financing does not depend on those retail buyers in the same way. That is a real offset. It does not replace the ownership units a turned cycle will need.

Chart: Active residential listings, Ontario vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

What it means

For builders: Quebec still has rising benchmarks and a ratio in balanced territory, which is the kind of comparable set that can support a presale. Ontario does not, and October's rate move does not help. I would not plan a national absorption number as if the demand problem stopped at the GTA border.

For policymakers: Ontario's resale "balance" is not proof the supply problem is solved. Sellers stopped listing. Builders stopped starting. Both are rational. Together they set up the next shortage. National inventory is about 197,000 listings, a little above CREA's long-term average of 190,000, with five months of supply. On paper, Canada looks balanced. Underneath, the biggest province is balancing by doing less, and the sales weakness that started in Toronto and Vancouver is no longer staying there. If we "solve" a glut by starting fewer homes, what does 2029 look like? The monthly CREA release will not answer that. The starts number might.

items.title: Firm Capital Buys Highlight Of Mississauga Project Under Creditor Protection For $74.3M
items.description:
A large condo project in Mississauga that became insolvent and was placed under creditor protection mid-construction over four years ago has officially been sold, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court.

The project is known as Highlight of Mississauga and is located at 4064, 4070, and 4078 Dixie Road, right across the street from Rockwood Mall in Mississauga.

The developer was a company called Hazelton Development Corporation (HDC) and the project website identifies an individual named Du Zhixian as the company’s President. Court documents also refer to him as Joe Du, and note that the company is majority-owned by “a prominent construction family in China.”

For the site, Hazelton Development Corporation was developing a 14-storey project with 265 strata units, including both condos and townhomes. Presales launched around May 2018 and 261 of 265 units were pre-sold, generating a total of $111,633,085 in revenue.

Construction commenced in September 2019 and completion was targeted for April 2021, but the project faced delays and liquidity issues that resulted in HDC seeking out creditor protection under the federal Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA) in April 2022, by which construction had reached Level 12.

The Debts

For the project, Hazelton took out a first-ranking mortgage with Meridian Credit Union in May 2019 for a construction loan with a principal amount of up to $50 million, plus a stand-by letter of credit facility up to $2 million.

It also took out a second mortgage with Centurion Mortgage Capital Corporation — which was folded into Centurion Asset Management in 2024 — for a construction facility of up to $19.9 million, plus a cost-overrun facility up to $3.5 million.

As of the time of their filing, HDC owed approximately $20,694,142 to Meridian and $20,673,626 to Centurion, for a total of $41,367,768, with interest continuing to accrue.

According to HDC, certain shareholders also loaned HDC approximately $6.35 million between September 2019 and March 2022, and a company called Triumph Eastern Investments Inc. also advanced six loans between October 2021 and March 2022.

Various amounts were also owed to contractors.

The Insolvency

Hazelton Development Corporation said they faced trouble from the onset as the COVID-19 pandemic hit just a few months after construction commenced. In March 2020, they notified purchasers that the project would be delayed. Construction later resumed, but HDC had to issue additional delay notices in May 2021, November 2021, January 2022, and March 2022.

“The initial construction budget for the Project was $101,183,823,” said HDC. “By November 2021, under previous management, the forecasted construction budget had increased by $11,672,011 to $113,669,237. These increases were due to, among other things: two significant delays on account of Covid-19 lock-downs, an increased level of supervision and project management, substantial increases to the hard costs budget for concrete, masonry, mechanical equipment and electrical work, and various material increases to the soft costs budget.”

Construction loan agreements often include obligations that borrowers maintain a minimum debt-to-equity ratio, but although HDC was able to raise additional equity from shareholders, it was not enough to satisfy Meridian’s requirement, and the lender ceased advances in July 2021, forcing HDC to rely on Centurion and buyer deposits.

In March 2022, the Du family bought out a group of shareholders, which gave them an 80% stake in HDC, and brought in new management to stabilize the project. A month later, in April 2022, HDC filed for creditor protection.

The Highlight of Mississauga as of March 2026. (Grant Thornton)

Under Creditor Protection

In July 2022, Toronto-based non-bank lender Firm Capital (TSX: FC) emerged as a sponsor and agreed to loan up to $80 million to pay off various debts and finance the construction of Highlight of Mississauga. The plan was approved, and construction then resumed.

In February 2023, the court then granted an order allowing the presale purchasers to be given two options. The first option would allow them to carry on with the purchase under revised terms, while the second option would terminate the presale agreement and see the buyer be compensated for their deposit with a 12% premium.

Although there were disputes with contractors and various other delays, construction continued and reached approximately 92.6% completion by February 2026, when the court-appointed Monitor said that “The ongoing deficiencies, construction challenges, weather-related delays, rising completion costs, and the Company’s funding constraints, have resulted in further delays to completion” and that “The Monitor understands that completion of the Project may no longer be feasible.”

By then, most of the presale purchasers had taken the compensation option and there were 197 unsold units. Lien claims by contractors had also continued to pile up, totalling to $10,802,325.

The Sale

The court-ordered sales process commenced in late-February. According to a report prepared by the Monitor, 15 parties signed confidentiality agreements and five toured the site. One party submitted a letter of intent in June, but reduced their offer during negotiations the following month, citing higher-than-anticipated expected taxes.

The Monitor then engaged other bidders, but could not find a better offer. Feedback from the market was that the project was better suited as a rental building, that the cost to complete was anywhere from $15 million to $30 million, and that the required remedial work was an added level of uncertainty.

“When it became apparent that there would be no unconditional bids,” said the Monitor, Firm Capital then began discussions to buy the project themselves through a reverse vesting order that would see them buy the shares of Hazelton Development Corporation — a share sale — instead of directly buying the real estate. Firm Capital’s purchase agreement also required that the remaining 48 presale contracts be terminated.

The purchase price is equivalent to the sum of various floating amounts, totalling to around $73.5 million, plus $802,000 in cash consideration, for a total of around $74.3 million estimated at September 30, 2026.

The sale approval court hearing was originally scheduled for October 1, but was then delayed due to various stakeholders raising objections. The hearing was delayed to October 22, then October 26, before it was finally approved by the Ontario Superior Court on November 4.

items.title: Bank Of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem Stepping Down
items.description:
Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem is stepping down next June.

The Bank’s Board of Directors announced Monday that Macklem has told them he won’t seek a second term when his seven-year term ends on June 2, 2027.

The Board has started a search for the next Governor.

“It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada,” Macklem said. “My time as Governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world. The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate.”

Macklem thanked the Board, the Minister of Finance, and the Prime Minister for entrusting him with the stewardship of Canada’s central bank.

“It is a privilege to serve as Governor, and I remain fully committed to fulfilling my responsibilities and delivering for Canadians through the remainder of my term,” he said.

The independent directors on the Board have formed a Search Committee to run the recruitment process. Executive recruiting firm Egon Zehnder is helping them, and the Bank is inviting interested candidates to read the Executive Brief for the role and contact Egon Zehnder confidentially.

The Bank expects to finish the search by spring 2027.

Subject to approval from the Minister of Finance and federal Cabinet, the Board’s independent directors will appoint the next Governor to a seven-year term starting June 3, 2027.

items.title: Supreme Court of Canada dismisses bid to appeal B.C. foreign buyer tax case
items.description:
The Supreme Court of Canada won't hear an appeal challenging the application of British Columbia's foreign buyer tax on a real estate purchase involving joint ownership by a Canadian citizen and a foreign national. 
 The B.C.
items._ogDesc: The Supreme Court of Canada won't hear an appeal challenging the application of British Columbia's foreign buyer tax on a real estate purchase involving joint ownership by a Canadian citizen and a foreign national. The B.C.
items.body:
The Supreme Court of Canada won't hear an appeal challenging the application of British Columbia's foreign buyer tax on a real estate purchase involving joint ownership by a Canadian citizen and a foreign national.

The B.C. Court of Appeal had previously dismissed an appeal brought by a couple who jointly bought an apartment in Richmond, B.C., putting 95 per cent in the Canadian woman's name, and five per cent in the name of her foreign partner.

But the man had actually paid 40 per cent of the purchase price, with the woman explaining the disparity by saying it was a Chinese custom for a husband to pay a "bride price" by buying his wife a home.

The couple, who were engaged in 2014 when they bought the home under a presale contract, paid the foreign buyer tax on only the five per cent registered to the foreign man, but an audit later found the tax "payable on the fair market value of the whole property."

The B.C. government had told the lower court the rule was meant to "prevent tax avoidance by foreign investors who own beneficial interests held indirectly by others."

The Supreme Court of Canada refused the couple leave to appeal on Thursday.

The couple had claimed imposing the tax on the entire value of the property was "profoundly unfair," but the three-judge panel of the Appeal Court found they could have avoided paying the tax on the property's entire value if they had registered ownership based on their contributions to the purchase price.

The appellate ruling from earlier this year said the man, Li-Yuan Chuang, paid 40 per cent of the purchase price, but registered only a five per cent stake in the property, which the couple declared to have a value of $474,500 at the time of purchase.

His Canadian partner, Chia-Wen Hsia, said it was "customary in Chinese culture to pay for ‘bride price’ as in the husband buying a house for the wife."

"In my husband’s case, he is not rich so he could only pay for part of the purchase price,” Hsia is quoted as saying in the appellate ruling.

The B.C. Supreme Court initially dismissed the couple's legal challenge in 2024.

The most recent assessed value for the two-bedroom apartment in the Avanti Richmond complex is $820,000.

The original B.C. Supreme Court ruling said a B.C. Finance Ministry tax analyst put the additional tax owed by the couple at just over $126,000.

The B.C. foreign buyer tax is 20 per cent of market value.

The couple's lawyer, Massao Morinaga, said they had no comment about the Supreme Court of Canada's dismissal of the case.

He said it was the "end of the road judicially," but the current foreign buyer tax legislation is drafted in a way that "captures situations that are inequitable."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

items.description:
VANCOUVER — British Columbia recorded 5,670 home sales last month, a drop of almost 11 per cent from October last year. 
 The B.C.
items._ogDesc: VANCOUVER — British Columbia recorded 5,670 home sales last month, a drop of almost 11 per cent from October last year. The B.C.
items.body:
VANCOUVER — British Columbia recorded 5,670 home sales last month, a drop of almost 11 per cent from October last year.

The B.C. Real Estate Association says in a statement that the average sale price of a home in the province this October fell about 2.8 per cent from about $977,000 last year to just short of $950,000.

The latest numbers come after the association released its fourth quarter forecast this week, projecting that B.C. home sales would slide 4.5 per cent this year from 2025 to about 67,000 units.

Association chief economist Brendon Ogmundson cites mounting market challenges from interest rates, slower immigration, oil-price shock and U.S. trade tensions, potentially contributing to the decline in the latest monthly numbers.

Ogmundson says more-affordable areas of the province have been resilient, with Kamloops seeing a 12 per cent rise in home sales last month.

But he says Metro Vancouver and the rest of the Lower Mainland continue to be hampered by "global headwinds and hawkish monetary policy," with Greater Vancouver sales falling 10 per cent to just over 2,000 units sold in October.

“Recoveries in more-expensive regions of the province are dependent on a retracing of rates and oil prices such that prospective buyers regain confidence after several volatile quarters,” Ogmundson says in the statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.
